items.entry: Most characters advance in the same class. However, you might decide to gain a level in another class using the rules in the "{@book Multiclassing|srd52|2|Multiclassing}" section later in this chapter.

items.name: Adjust Hit Points and Hit Point Dice
entries: Each time you gain a level, you gain an additional Hit Die. Roll that die, add your Constitution modifier to the roll, and add the total (minimum of 1) to your Hit Point maximum. Instead of rolling, you can use the fixed value shown in the Fixed Hit Points by Class table.

entries.caption: Fixed Hit Points by Class
rows: {@class Bard|srd52}, {@class Cleric|srd52}, {@class Druid|srd52}, {@class Monk|srd52}, {@class Rogue|srd52}, or {@class Warlock|srd52}

items.name: Record New Class Features
items.entry: Look at your class features table in {@book Classes|srd52|3} and note the features you gain at your new level in that class. Make any choices offered by a new feature.

items.name: Adjust Proficiency Bonus
items.entry: A character's Proficiency Bonus increases at certain levels, as shown in the {@book Character Advancement table|srd52|2|Character Advancement} and your class features table in {@book Classes|srd52|3}. When your Proficiency Bonus increases, increase all the numbers on your character sheet that include your Proficiency Bonus.

items.name: Adjust Ability Modifiers
items.entry: If you choose a feat that increases one or more of your ability scores, your ability modifier also changes if the new score is an even number. When that happens, adjust all the numbers on your character sheet that use that ability modifier. When your Constitution modifier increases by 1, your Hit Point maximum increases by 1 for each level you have attained. For example, if a character reaches level 8 and increases their Constitution score from 17 to 18, the Constitution modifier increases to +4. The character's Hit Point maximum then increases by 8, in addition to the Hit Points gained for reaching level 8.

entries.name: Tiers of Play
entries: With each new level, characters acquire new capabilities that equip them to handle greater challenges. As characters advance in level, the tone of the game also changes, and the stakes of the campaign get higher. It's helpful to think of a character's (and a campaign's) arc in terms of four tiers of play, describing the journey from a level 1 character just beginning an adventuring career to the epic heights of level 20. These tiers don't have any rules associated with them; they point to the fact that the play experience evolves as characters gain levels.

entries.name: Tier 1 (Levels 1–4)
entries: In tier 1, characters are apprentice adventurers, though they are already set apart from the broader populace by virtue of their extraordinary abilities. They learn their starting class features and choose a subclass. The threats they face usually pose a danger to local farmsteads or villages.

entries.name: Tier 2 (Levels 5–10)
entries: In tier 2, characters are full-fledged adventurers. Spellcasters gain iconic spells such as {@spell Fireball|srd52}, {@spell Lightning Bolt|srd52}, and {@spell Raise Dead|srd52}. Most weapon-focused classes gain the ability to make multiple attacks in a round. The characters now face dangers that threaten cities and kingdoms.

entries.name: Tier 3 (Levels 11–16)
entries: In tier 3, characters have reached a level of power that makes them special among adventurers. At level 11, many spellcasters learn reality-altering spells. Other characters gain features that allow them to make more attacks or to do more impressive things with those attacks. These adventurers often confront threats to whole regions.

entries.name: Tier 4 (Levels 17–20)
entries: At tier 4, characters achieve the pinnacle of their class features, becoming heroic archetypes. The fate of the world or even the order of the multiverse might hang in the balance during their adventures.

entries.name: Bonus Feats at Level 20
entries: A DM can use feats as a form of advancement after characters reach level 20 to provide greater power to characters who have no more levels to gain. With this approach, each character gains one feat of their choice for every 30,000 XP the character earns above 355,000 XP. {@book Epic Boon|srd52|5|Epic Boon Feats} feats are especially appropriate for these bonus feats, but a player can choose any feat for which their level 20 character qualifies.

entries.name: Starting at Higher Levels
entries: Your DM might start your group's characters at a level higher than 1. It is particularly recommended to start at level 3 if your group is composed of seasoned players.

entries.name: Creating Your Character
entries: Creating a higher-level character uses the same character-creation steps outlined in this chapter and the rules for advancing beyond level 1 provided in the "{@book Level Advancement|srd52|2|Level Advancement}" section. You begin with the minimum amount of XP required to reach your starting level. For example, if the GM starts you at level 10, you have 64,000 XP.

entries.name: Starting Equipment
entries: The GM decides whether your character starts with more than the standard equipment for a level 1 character, possibly even one or more magic items. The Starting Equipment at Higher Levels table is a guide for the GM.

Also, check with your GM about what equipment is available for you to buy with your starting money. For example, the firearms described in {@book Equipment|srd52|6|Weapons} are too expensive for level 1 characters, but they might be available for purchase if your GM allows them.

entries.caption: Starting Equipment at Higher Levels
rows: 500 GP plus {@dice 1d10 × 25} GP plus normal starting equipment
5,000 gp plus {@dice 1d10 × 250} GP plus normal starting equipment
20,000 GP plus {@dice 1d10 × 250} GP plus normal starting equipment
2 {@filter Common|items|rarity=Common}, 4 {@filter Uncommon|items|rarity=Uncommon}, 3 {@filter Rare|items|rarity=Rare}, 1 {@filter Very Rare|items|rarity=Very Rare}

entries.name: Multiclassing
entries: Multiclassing allows you to gain levels in multiple classes. With this rule, you have the option of gaining a level in a new class whenever you advance in level instead of gaining a level in your current class. Doing so lets you mix the abilities of those classes to realize a character concept that might not be reflected in a single class.

entries.name: Prerequisites
entries: To qualify for a new class, you must have a score of at least 13 in the primary ability of the new class and your current classes. For example, a Barbarian who decides to multiclass into the Druid class must have Strength and Wisdom scores of 13 or higher, since Strength is the primary ability for Barbarians and Wisdom is the primary ability for Druids.

entries.name: Experience Points
entries: The Experience Point cost to gain a level is based on your total character level, not your level in a particular class, as shown in the {@book Character Advancement table|srd52|2|Character Advancement} in this chapter. For example, if you are a level 6 Cleric / level 1 Fighter, you must gain enough XP to reach level 8 before you can take your second level as a Fighter or your seventh level as a Cleric.

entries.name: Hit Points and Hit Point Dice
entries: You gain the Hit Points from your new class as described for levels after 1. You gain the level 1 Hit Points for a class only when your total character level is 1.

Add together the Hit Dice granted by all your classes to form your pool of Hit Dice. If these dice are the same die type, you can pool them together. For example, both the Fighter and the Paladin have a {@dice d10} Hit Die, so if you are a level 5 Fighter / level 5 Paladin, you have ten {@dice d10} Hit Dice. If your classes give you Hit Dice of different types, track them separately. If you are a level 5 Cleric / level 5 Paladin, for example, you have five {@dice d8} Hit Dice and five {@dice d10} Hit Dice.

entries.name: Proficiency Bonus
entries: Your Proficiency Bonus is based on your total character level, not your level in a particular class, as shown in the {@book Character Advancement table|srd52|2|Character Advancement}. For example, if you are a level 3 Fighter / level 2 Rogue, you have the Proficiency Bonus of a level 5 character, which is +3.

entries.name: Proficiencies
entries: When you gain your first level in a class other than your initial class, you gain only some of the new class's starting proficiencies, as detailed in each class's description in {@book Classes|srd52|3}.

entries.name: Class Features
entries: When you gain a new level in a class, you get its features for that level. A few features have additional rules when you're multiclassing. Check the information about multiclassing included in each of your classes' descriptions.
Special rules apply to Extra Attack, Spellcasting, and features (such as Unarmored Defense) that give you alternative ways to calculate your Armor Class.

entries.name: Armor Class
entries: If you have multiple ways to calculate your {@variantrule Armor Class|srd52}, you can benefit from only one at a time. For example, a Monk/Sorcerer with a Monk's Unarmored Defense feature and a Sorcerer's Draconic Resilience feature must choose only one of those features as a way to calculate Armor Class.

entries.name: Extra Attack
entries: If you gain the Extra Attack feature from more than one class, the features don't stack. You can't make more than two attacks with this feature unless you have a feature that says you can (such as the Fighter's Two Extra Attacks feature).
Similarly, the Warlock's Thirsting Blade invocation, which grants you the Extra Attack feature with your pact weapon, doesn't give you additional attacks if you also have Extra Attack.

entries.name: Spellcasting
entries: Your capacity for spellcasting depends partly on your combined levels in all your spellcasting classes and partly on your individual levels in those classes. Once you have the Spellcasting feature from more than one class, use the rules below. If you multiclass but have the Spellcasting feature from only one class, follow the rules for that class.

entries.caption: Multiclass Spellcaster: Spell Slots per Spell Level

entries.name: Spells Prepared
entries: You determine what spells you can prepare for each class individually, as if you were a single-classed member of that class. If you are a level 4 Ranger / level 3 Sorcerer, for example, you can prepare five level 1 Ranger spells, and you can prepare six Sorcerer spells of level 1 or 2 (as well as four Sorcerer cantrips).
Each spell you prepare is associated with one of your classes, and you use the spellcasting ability of that class when you cast the spell.

entries.name: Cantrips
entries: If a cantrip of yours increases in power at higher levels, the increase is based on your total character level, not your level in a particular class, unless the spell says otherwise.

entries.name: Spell Slots
entries: You determine your available spell slots by adding together the following:

items: All your levels in the Bard, Cleric, Druid, Sorcerer, and Wizard classes
Half your levels (round up) in the Paladin and Ranger classes
One third of your Fighter or Rogue levels (round down) if you have the Eldritch Knight or Arcane Trickster subclass.

entries: Then look up this total level in the Level column of the Multiclass Spellcaster table. You use the slots for that level to cast spells of an appropriate level from any class whose Spellcasting feature you have.

This table might give you spell slots of a higher level than the spells you prepare. You can use those slots but only to cast your lower-level spells. If a lower-level spell that you cast, like {@spell Burning Hands|srd52}, has an enhanced effect when cast at a higher level, you can use the enhanced effect as normal.

For example, if you are a level 4 Ranger / level 3 Sorcerer, you count as a level 5 character when determining your spell slots, counting all your levels as a Sorcerer and half your Ranger levels. As shown in the Multiclass Spellcaster table, you have four level 1 spell slots, three level 2 slots, and two level 3 slots. However, you can't prepare any level 3 spells, nor can you prepare any level 2 Ranger spells. You can use the spell slots of those levels to cast the spells you do prepare—and potentially enhance their effects.

entries.name: Pact Magic
entries: If you have the Pact Magic feature from the Warlock class and the Spellcasting feature, you can use the spell slots you gain from Pact Magic to cast spells you have prepared from classes with the Spellcasting feature, and you can use the spell slots you gain from the Spellcasting feature to cast Warlock spells you have prepared.

entries.name: Trinkets
entries: When you make your character, you can roll once on the {@item Trinket|srd52|Trinkets} table to gain a Tiny trinket, a simple item lightly touched by mystery. The GM might also use this table. It can help stock a room in a dungeon or fill a creature's pockets.

entries.name: Character Backgrounds
entries: Your character's background is a collection of characteristics that represent the place and occupation that were most formative before your character embarked on a life of adventure.

entries.name: Parts of a Background
entries: A background includes the following parts.

entries.name: Ability Scores
entries: A background lists three of your character's ability scores. Increase one by 2 and another one by 1, or increase all three by 1. None of these increases can raise a score above 20.

entries.name: Feat
entries: A background gives your character a specified Origin feat (described in {@book Feats|srd52|5}).

entries.name: Skill Proficiencies
entries: A background gives your character proficiency in two specified skills.

entries.name: Tool Proficiency
entries: Each background gives a character proficiency with one tool—either a specific tool or one chosen from the Artisan's Tools category. Tools are detailed in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}".

entries.name: Equipment
entries: Each background offers a choice between a package of equipment and 50 GP.

entries.name: Character Species
entries: When you choose your character's species, you determine whether your character is a human or a member of a fantastical species, such as dragonborn or gnome.

The peoples of the multiverse hail from different worlds and include many kinds of sapient life forms. A player character's species is the set of game traits that an adventurer gains from being one of those life forms.

Some species can trace their origin to a single world, plane of existence, or god, while other species first appeared in multiple realms at once. Whatever a species' genesis, its members have spread across the multiverse and contribute to many different cultures.

Members of most species live for about 80 years, with exceptions noted in the text about the species in "{@book Character Origins|srd52|4}". Regardless of life span, members of all species reach physical maturity at about the same age. Your character can be any age that isn't beyond their species' normal life span.

entries.name: Parts of a Species
entries: A species includes the following parts.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: A character's species determines the character's creature type, which is described in the {@book Rules Glossary|srd52|10}. Every species in "{@book Character Origins|srd52|4}" is Humanoid; playable non-Humanoid species appear in other books.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your character's species determines the character's size. Individuals within a species cover a wide range of heights, and some species include such diversity of size that you can choose whether your character is Small or Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: Your character's species determines the character's Speed.

entries.name: Special Traits
entries: Each species gives a character special traits—unique characteristics based on the species' physiology or magical nature. When you choose a species, your character gets all the special traits listed for it. Some traits involve making a choice from a handful of options.

entries.name: Feat Descriptions
entries: The feats that follow are organized by category— Origin, General, Fighting Style, or Epic Boon—and alphabetized in each category.

entries.name: Parts of a Feat
entries: The description of a feat contains the following parts, which are presented after the feat's name.

entries.name: Category
entries: A feat is a member of a category, which is noted in the feat. If you're instructed to choose a feat from a specific category, such as the Origin category, that category must appear under the feat's name. If you're instructed to choose a feat and no category is specified, you can choose from any category.

entries.name: Prerequisite
entries: To take a feat, you must meet any prerequisite in its description unless a feature allows you to take the feat without the prerequisite. If a prerequisite includes a class, you must have at least 1 level in that class to take the feat.

entries.name: Benefit
entries: The benefits of a feat are detailed after any prerequisites are listed. If you have a feat, you gain its benefits.

entries.name: Repeatable
entries: A feat can be taken only once unless its description states otherwise in a "Repeatable" subsection.

entries.name: Selling Equipment
entries: Equipment fetches half its cost when sold. In contrast, trade goods and valuables—like gems and art objects—retain their full value in the marketplace. "{@book Magic Items|srd52|11}" has prices for magic items.

entries.name: Coins
entries: Characters often find coins on their adventures and can spend those coins in shops, inns, and other businesses. Coins come in different denominations based on the relative worth of their material. The Coin Values table lists coins and how much they're worth relative to the Gold Piece, which is the game's main coin. For example, 100 Copper Pieces are worth 1 Gold Piece.
A coin weighs about a third of an ounce, so fifty coins weigh a pound.

entries.name: Weapons
entries: The Weapons table in this section shows the game's main weapons. The table lists the cost and weight of each weapon, as well as the following details:

items.name: Category
items.entry: Every weapon falls into a category: Simple or Martial. Weapon proficiencies are usually tied to one of these categories. For example, you might have proficiency with Simple weapons.

items.name: Melee or Ranged
items.entry: A weapon is classified as either Melee or Ranged. A Melee weapon is used to attack a target within 5 feet, whereas a Ranged weapon is used to attack at a greater distance.

items.name: Damage
items.entry: The table lists the amount of damage a weapon deals when an attacker hits with it as well as the type of that damage.

items.name: Properties
items.entry: Any properties a weapon has are listed in the Properties column. Each property is defined in the "{@book Properties|srd52|6|Properties}" section.

items.name: Mastery
items.entry: Each weapon has a mastery property, which is defined in the "{@book Mastery Properties|srd52|6|Mastery Properties}" section. To use that property, you must have a feature that lets you use it.

entries.name: Weapon Proficiency
entries: Anyone can wield a weapon, but you must have proficiency with it to add your Proficiency Bonus to an attack roll you make with it. A player character's features can provide weapon proficiencies. A monster is proficient with any weapon in its stat block.

entries.name: Properties
entries: Here are definitions of the properties in the Properties column of the Weapons table.

entries.name: Ammunition
entries: You can use a weapon that has the Ammunition property to make a ranged attack only if you have ammunition to fire from it. The type of ammunition required is specified with the weapon's range. Each attack expends one piece of ammunition. Drawing the ammunition is part of the attack (you need a free hand to load a one-handed weapon). After a fight, you can spend 1 minute to recover half the ammunition (round down) you used in the fight; the rest is lost.

entries.name: Finesse
entries: When making an attack with a Finesse weapon, use your choice of your Strength or Dexterity modifier for the attack and damage rolls. You must use the same modifier for both rolls.

entries.name: Heavy
entries: You have {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on attack rolls with a Heavy weapon if it's a Melee weapon and your Strength score isn't at least 13 or if it's a Ranged weapon and your Dexterity score isn't at least 13.

entries.name: Improvised Weapons
entries: If you use an object—such as a table leg, frying pan, or bottle—as a makeshift weapon, see "{@variantrule Improvised Weapons|srd52}" in the {@book rules glossary|srd52|10|Improvised Weapons}. Also see those rules if you wield a weapon in an unusual way, such as using a Ranged weapon to make a melee attack.

entries.name: Light
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action on your turn and attack with a Light weapon, you can make one extra attack as a Bonus Action later on the same turn. That extra attack must be made with a different Light weapon, and you don't add your ability modifier to the extra attack's damage unless that modifier is negative. For example, you can attack with a {@item Shortsword|srd52} in one hand and a {@item Dagger|srd52} in the other using the {@action Attack|srd52} action and a Bonus Action, but you don't add your Strength or Dexterity modifier to the damage roll of the Bonus Action unless that modifier is negative.

entries.name: Loading
entries: You can fire only one piece of ammunition from a Loading weapon when you use an action, a Bonus Action, or a Reaction to fire it, regardless of the number of attacks you can normally make.

entries.name: Range
entries: A Range weapon has a range in parentheses after the {@itemProperty A|srd52|Ammunition} or {@itemProperty T|srd52|Thrown} property. The range lists two numbers. The first is the weapon's normal range in feet, and the second is the weapon's long range. When attacking a target beyond normal range, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on the attack roll. You can't attack a target beyond the long range.

entries.name: Reach
entries: A Reach weapon adds 5 feet to your reach when you attack with it, as well as when determining your reach for {@action opportunity attack|srd52|Opportunity Attacks} with it.

entries.name: Thrown
entries: If a weapon has the Thrown property, you can throw the weapon to make a ranged attack, and you can draw that weapon as part of the attack. If the weapon is a Melee weapon, use the same ability modifier for the attack and damage rolls that you use for a melee attack with that weapon.

entries.name: Two-Handed
entries: A Two-Handed weapon requires two hands when you attack with it.

entries.name: Versatile
entries: A Versatile weapon can be used with one or two hands. A damage value in parentheses appears with the property. The weapon deals that damage when used with two hands to make a melee attack.

entries.name: Mastery Properties
entries: Each weapon has a mastery property, which is usable only by a character who has a feature, such as Weapon Mastery, that unlocks the property for the character. The properties are defined below.

entries.name: Cleave
entries: If you hit a creature with a melee attack roll using this weapon, you can make a melee attack roll with the weapon against a second creature within 5 feet of the first that is also within your reach. On a hit, the second creature takes the weapon's damage, but don't add your ability modifier to that damage unless that modifier is negative. You can make this extra attack only once per turn.

entries.name: Graze
entries: If your attack roll with this weapon misses a creature, you can deal damage to that creature equal to the ability modifier you used to make the attack roll. This damage is the same type dealt by the weapon, and the damage can be increased only by increasing the ability modifier.

entries.name: Nick
entries: When you make the extra attack of the {@itemProperty L|srd52|Light} property, you can make it as part of the {@action Attack|srd52} action instead of as a Bonus Action. You can make this extra attack only once per turn.

entries.name: Push
entries: If you hit a creature with this weapon, you can push the creature up to 10 feet straight away from yourself if it is Large or smaller.

entries.name: Sap
entries: If you hit a creature with this weapon, that creature has {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on its next attack roll before the start of your next turn.

entries.name: Slow
entries: If you hit a creature with this weapon and deal damage to it, you can reduce its Speed by 10 feet until the start of your next turn. If the creature is hit more than once by weapons that have this property, the Speed reduction doesn't exceed 10 feet.

entries.name: Topple
entries: If you hit a creature with this weapon, you can force the creature to make a Constitution saving throw ({@dc 8} plus the ability modifier used to make the attack roll and your Proficiency Bonus). On a failed save, the creature has the {@condition Prone|srd52} condition.

entries.name: Vex
entries: If you hit a creature with this weapon and deal damage to the creature, you have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on your next attack roll against that creature before the end of your next turn.

entries.name: Armor
entries: The Armor table lists the game's main armor. The table includes the cost and weight of armor, as well as the following details:

items.name: Category
items.entry: Every type of armor falls into a category: Light, Medium, or Heavy. The category determines how long it takes to don or doff the armor (as shown in the table).

entries: {@b Armor Class (AC}). The table's Armor Class column tells you what your base AC is when you wear a type of armor. For example, if you wear Leather Armor, your base AC is 11 plus your Dexterity modifier, whereas your AC is 16 in Chain Mail.

items.name: Strength
items.entry: If the table shows a Strength score in the Strength column for an armor type, that armor reduces the wearer's speed by 10 feet unless the wearer has a Strength score equal to or higher than the listed score.

items.name: Stealth
items.entry: If the table shows "Disadvantage" in the Stealth column for an armor type, the wearer has {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|srd52}) checks.

rows.entry: {@i Light Armor (1 Minute to Don or Doff)}
{@i Medium Armor (5 Minutes to Don and 1 Minute to Doff)}
{@i Heavy Armor (10 Minutes to Don and 5 Minutes to Doff)}
{@i Shield ({@action Utilize|srd52} Action to Don or Doff)}

entries.name: Armor Training
entries: Anyone can don armor or hold a Shield, but only those with training can use them effectively, as explained below. A character's class and other features determine the character's armor training. A monster has training with any armor in its stat block.

entries.name: Light, Medium, or Heavy Armor
entries: If you wear Light, Medium, or Heavy armor and lack training with it, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on any {@variantrule D20 Test|srd52} that involves Strength or Dexterity, and you can't cast spells.

entries.name: Shield
entries: You gain the Armor Class benefit of a Shield only if you have training with it.

entries.name: One at a Time
entries: A creature can wear only one suit of armor at a time and wield only one Shield at a time.

entries.name: Tools
entries: A tool helps you make specialized ability checks, craft certain items, or both. A tool's description includes the tool's cost and weight, as well as the following entries:

items.name: Ability
items.entry: This entry lists the ability to use when making an ability check with the tool.

items.name: Utilize
items.entry: This entry lists things you can do with the tool when you take the {@action Utilize|srd52} action. You can do one of those things each time you take the action. This entry also provides the DC for the action.

items.name: Craft
items.entry: This entry lists what, if anything, you can craft with the tool. For crafting rules, see "{@book Crafting Nonmagical Items|srd52|6|Crafting Nonmagical Items}," "{@book Brewing Potions of Healing|srd52|6|Brewing Potions of Healing}," and "{@book Scribing Spell Scrolls|srd52|6|Scribing Spell Scrolls}" later in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}".

items.name: Variants
items.entry: This entry appears if the tool has variants, which are listed. Each requires a separate proficiency.

entries.name: Tool Proficiency
entries: If you have proficiency with a tool, add your Proficiency Bonus to any ability check you make that uses the tool. If you have proficiency in a skill that's used with that check, you have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on the check too.
Your features might give you proficiency with a tool. A monster has proficiency with any tool in its stat block.

entries.name: Adventuring Gear
entries: The Adventuring Gear table in this section includes gear that adventurers often find useful. These items are described here in alphabetical order, with an item's price appearing after its name.

entries.caption: Adventuring Gear
rows: {@item Map or Scroll Case|srd52|Case, Map or Scroll}

entries.name: Acid (25 GP)
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action, you can replace one of your attacks with throwing a vial of Acid. Target one creature or object you can see within 20 feet of yourself. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw ({@dc 8} plus your Dexterity modifier and Proficiency Bonus) or take {@dice 2d6} Acid damage.

entries.name: Alchemist's Fire (50 GP)
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action, you can replace one of your attacks with throwing a flask of Alchemist's Fire. Target one creature or object you can see within 20 feet of yourself. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw ({@dc 8} plus your Dexterity modifier and Proficiency Bonus) or take {@dice 1d4} Fire damage and start {@hazard burning|srd52}.

entries.name: Ammunition (Varies)
entries: Ammunition is required by a weapon that has the {@itemProperty A|srd52|Ammunition} property. A weapon's description specifies the type of ammunition used by the weapon. The Ammunition table lists the different types and the amount you get when you buy them. The table also lists the item that is typically used to store each type; storage must be bought separately.

entries.name: Antitoxin (50 GP)
entries: As a Bonus Action, you can drink a vial of Antitoxin to gain {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on saving throws to avoid or end the {@condition Poisoned|srd52} condition for 1 hour.

entries.name: Arcane Focus (Varies)
entries: An Arcane Focus takes one of the forms in the Arcane Focuses table and is bejeweled or carved to channel arcane magic. A Sorcerer, Warlock, or Wizard can use such an item as a {@variantrule Spellcasting Focus|srd52}.

entries.name: Backpack (2 GP)
entries: A Backpack holds up to 30 pounds within 1 cubic foot. It can also serve as a saddlebag.

entries.name: Ball Bearings (1 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can spill Ball Bearings from their pouch. They spread to cover a level, 10-foot-square area within 10 feet of yourself. A creature that enters this area for the first time on a turn must succeed on a {@dc 10} Dexterity saving throw or have the {@condition Prone|srd52} condition. It takes 10 minutes to recover the Ball Bearings.

entries.name: Barrel (2 GP)
entries: A Barrel holds up to 40 gallons of liquid or up to 4 cubic feet of dry goods.

entries.name: Basket (4 SP)
entries: A Basket holds up to 40 pounds within 2 cubic feet.

entries.name: Bedroll (1 GP)
entries: A Bedroll sleeps one Small or Medium creature. While in a Bedroll, you automatically succeed on saving throws against extreme cold (see "{@book Gameplay Toolbox|srd52|10}").

entries.name: Bell (1 GP)
entries: When rung as a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, a Bell produces a sound that can be heard up to 60 feet away.

entries.name: Blanket (5 SP)
entries: While wrapped in a blanket, you have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on saving throws against extreme cold (see "{@book Gameplay Toolbox|srd52|10}").

entries.name: Block and Tackle (1 GP)
entries: A Block and Tackle allows you to hoist up to four times the weight you can normally lift.

entries.name: Book (25 GP)
entries: A Book contains fiction or nonfiction. If you consult an accurate nonfiction Book about its topic, you gain a +5 bonus to Intelligence ({@skill Arcana|srd52}, {@skill History|srd52}, {@skill Nature|srd52}, or {@skill Religion|srd52}) checks you make about that topic.

entries.name: Bottle, Glass (2 GP)
entries: A Glass Bottle holds up to 1½ pints.

entries.name: Bucket (5 CP)
entries: A Bucket holds up to half a cubic foot of contents.

entries.name: Burglar's Pack (16 GP)
entries: A Burglar's Pack contains the following items: {@item Backpack|srd52}, {@item Ball Bearings|srd52}, {@item Bell|srd52}, 10 {@item Candle|srd52|Candles}, {@item Crowbar|srd52}, {@item Hooded Lantern|srd52}, 7 flasks of {@item Oil|srd52}, 5 days of {@item Rations|srd52}, {@item Rope|srd52}, {@item Tinderbox|srd52}, and {@item Waterskin|srd52}.

entries.name: Caltrops (1 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can spread Caltrops from their bag to cover a 5-foot-square area within 5 feet of yourself. A creature that enters this area for the first time on a turn must succeed on a {@dc 15} Dexterity saving throw or take 1 Piercing damage and have its Speed reduced to 0 until the start of its next turn. It takes 10 minutes to recover the Caltrops.

entries.name: Candle (1 CP)
entries: For 1 hour, a lit Candle sheds {@variantrule Bright Light|srd52} in a 5-foot radius and {@variantrule Dim Light|srd52} for an additional 5 feet.

entries.name: Case, Crossbow Bolt (1 GP)
entries: A Crossbow Bolt Case holds up to 20 {@item Bolts (20)|srd52|Bolts}.

entries.name: Case, Map or Scroll (1 GP)
entries: A Map or Scroll Case holds up to 10 sheets of {@item paper|srd52} or 5 sheets of {@item parchment|srd52}.

entries.name: Chain (5 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can wrap a Chain around an unwilling creature within 5 feet of yourself that has the {@condition Grappled|srd52}, {@condition Incapacitated|srd52}, or {@condition Restrained|srd52} condition if you succeed on a {@dc 13} Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check. If the creature's legs are bound, the creature has the Restrained condition until it escapes. Escaping the Chain requires the creature to make a successful {@dc 18} Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|srd52}) check as an action. Bursting the Chain requires a successful {@dc 20} Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check as an action.

entries.name: Chest (5 GP)
entries: A Chest holds up to 12 cubic feet of contents.

entries.name: Climber's Kit (25 GP)
entries: A Climber's Kit includes boot tips, gloves, pitons, and a harness. As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can use the Climber's Kit to anchor yourself; when you do, you can't fall more than 25 feet from the anchor point, and you can't move more than 25 feet from there without undoing the anchor as a Bonus Action.

entries.name: Clothes, Fine (15 GP)
entries: Fine Clothes are made of expensive fabrics and adorned with expertly crafted details. Some events and locations admit only people wearing these clothes.

entries.name: Clothes, Traveler's (2 GP)
entries: Traveler's Clothes are resilient garments designed for travel in various environments.

entries.name: Component Pouch (25 GP)
entries: A Component Pouch is watertight and filled with compartments that hold all the free Material components of your spells.

entries.name: Costume (5 GP)
entries: While wearing a Costume, you have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on any ability check you make to impersonate the person or type of person it represents.

entries.name: Crowbar (2 GP)
entries: Using a Crowbar gives you {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on Strength checks where the Crowbar's leverage can be applied.

entries.name: Diplomat's Pack (39 GP)
entries: A Diplomat's Pack contains the following items: {@item Chest|srd52}, {@item Fine Clothes|srd52}, {@item Ink|srd52}, 5 {@item Ink Pen|srd52|Ink Pens}, {@item Lamp|srd52}, 2 {@item Map or Scroll Case|srd52|Map or Scroll Cases}, 4 flasks of {@item Oil|srd52}, 5 sheets of {@item Paper|srd52}, 5 sheets of {@item Parchment|srd52}, {@item Perfume|srd52}, and {@item Tinderbox|srd52}.

entries.name: Druidic Focus (Varies)
entries: A Druidic Focus takes one of the forms in the Druidic Focuses table and is carved, tied with ribbon, or painted to channel primal magic. A Druid or Ranger can use such an object as a {@variantrule Spellcasting Focus|srd52}.

entries.name: Dungeoneer's Pack (12 GP)
entries: A Dungeoneer's Pack contains the following items: {@item Backpack|srd52}, {@item Caltrops|srd52}, {@item Crowbar|srd52}, 2 flasks of {@item Oil|srd52}, 10 days of {@item Rations|srd52}, {@item Rope|srd52}, {@item Tinderbox|srd52}, 10 {@item Torch|srd52|Torches}, and {@item Waterskin|srd52}.

entries.name: Entertainer's Pack (40 GP)
entries: An Entertainer's Pack contains the following items: {@item Backpack|srd52}, {@item Bedroll|srd52}, {@item Bell|srd52}, {@item Bullseye Lantern|srd52}, 3 {@item Costume|srd52|Costumes}, {@item Mirror|srd52}, 8 flasks of {@item Oil|srd52}, 9 days of {@item Rations|srd52}, {@item Tinderbox|srd52}, and {@item Waterskin|srd52}.

entries.name: Explorer's Pack (10 GP)
entries: An Explorer's Pack contains the following items: {@item Backpack|srd52}, {@item Bedroll|srd52}, 2 flasks of {@item Oil|srd52}, 10 days of {@item Rations|srd52}, {@item Rope|srd52}, {@item Tinderbox|srd52}, 10 {@item Torch|srd52|Torches}, and {@item Waterskin|srd52}.

entries.name: Flask (2 CP)
entries: A Flask holds up to 1 pint.

entries.name: Grappling Hook (2 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can throw the Grappling Hook at a railing, a ledge, or another catch within 50 feet of yourself, and the hook catches on if you succeed on a {@dc 13} Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|srd52}) check. If you tied a {@item Rope|srd52} to the hook, you can then climb it.

entries.name: Healer's Kit (5 GP)
entries: A Healer's Kit has ten uses. As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can expend one of its uses to stabilize an {@condition Unconscious|srd52} creature that has 0 Hit Points without needing to make a Wisdom ({@skill Medicine|srd52}) check.

entries.name: Holy Symbol (Varies)
entries: A Holy Symbol takes one of the forms in the Holy Symbol table and is bejeweled or painted to channel divine magic. A Cleric or Paladin can use a Holy Symbol as a {@variantrule Spellcasting Focus|srd52}.
The table indicates whether a Holy Symbol needs to be held, worn, or borne on fabric (such as a tabard or banner) or a Shield.

entries.caption: Holy Symbols
rows: {@item Emblem|srd52} (borne on fabric or a Shield)

entries.name: Holy Water (25 GP)
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action, you can replace one of your attacks with throwing a flask of Holy Water. Target one creature you can see within 20 feet of yourself. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw ({@dc 8} plus your Dexterity modifier and Proficiency Bonus) or take {@dice 2d8} Radiant damage if it is a Fiend or an Undead.

entries.name: Hunting Trap (5 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can set a Hunting Trap, which is a sawtooth steel ring that snaps shut when a creature steps on a pressure plate in the center. The trap is affixed by a heavy chain to an immobile object, such as a tree or a spike driven into the ground. A creature that steps on the plate must succeed on a {@dc 13} Dexterity saving throw or take {@dice 1d4} Piercing damage and have its Speed reduced to 0 until the start of its next turn. Thereafter, until the creature breaks free of the trap, its movement is limited by the length of the chain (typically 3 feet). A creature can use its action to make a {@dc 13} Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check, freeing itself or another creature within its reach on a success. Each failed check deals 1 Piercing damage to the trapped creature.

entries.name: Ink (10 GP)
entries: Ink comes in a 1-ounce bottle, which provides enough ink to write about 500 pages.

entries.name: Ink Pen (2 CP)
entries: Using {@item Ink|srd52}, an Ink Pen is used to write or draw.

entries.name: Jug (2 CP)
entries: A Jug holds up to 1 gallon.

entries.name: Ladder (1 SP)
entries: A Ladder is 10 feet tall. You must climb to move up or down it.

entries.name: Lamp (5 SP)
entries: A Lamp burns {@item Oil|srd52} as fuel to cast {@variantrule Bright Light|srd52} in a 15-foot radius and {@variantrule Dim Light|srd52} for an additional 30 feet.

entries.name: Lantern, Bullseye (10 GP)
entries: A Bullseye Lantern burns {@item Oil|srd52} as fuel to cast {@variantrule Bright Light|srd52} in a 60-foot {@variantrule Cone [Area of Effect]|srd52|Cone} and {@variantrule Dim Light|srd52} for an additional 60 feet.

entries.name: Lantern, Hooded (5 GP)
entries: A Hooded Lantern burns {@item Oil|srd52} as fuel to cast {@variantrule Bright Light|srd52} in a 30-foot radius and {@variantrule Dim Light|srd52} for an additional 30 feet. As a Bonus Action, you can lower the hood, reducing the light to Dim Light in a 5-foot radius, or raise it again.

entries.name: Lock (10 GP)
entries: A Lock comes with a key. Without the key, a creature can use {@item Thieves' Tools|srd52} to pick this Lock with a successful {@dc 15} Dexterity ({@skill Sleight of Hand|srd52}) check.

entries.name: Magnifying Glass (100 GP)
entries: A Magnifying Glass grants {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on any ability check made to appraise or inspect a highly detailed item. Lighting a fire with a Magnifying Glass requires light as bright as sunlight to focus, tinder to ignite, and about 5 minutes for the fire to ignite.

entries.name: Manacles (2 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can use Manacles to bind an unwilling Small or Medium creature within 5 feet of yourself that has the {@condition Grappled|srd52}, {@condition Incapacitated|srd52}, or {@condition Restrained|srd52} condition if you succeed on a {@dc 13} Dexterity ({@skill Sleight of Hand|srd52}) check. While bound, a creature has {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on attack rolls, and the creature is {@condition Restrained|srd52} if the Manacles are attached to a chain or hook that is fixed in place. Escaping the Manacles requires a successful {@dc 20} Dexterity ({@skill Sleight of Hand|srd52}) check as an action. Bursting them requires a successful {@dc 25} Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check as an action.

Each set of Manacles comes with a key. Without the key, a creature can use {@item Thieves' Tools|srd52} to pick the Manacles' lock with a successful {@dc 15} Dexterity ({@skill Sleight of Hand|srd52}) check.

entries.name: Map (1 GP)
entries: If you consult an accurate Map, you gain a +5 bonus to Wisdom ({@skill Survival|srd52}) checks you make to find your way in the place represented on it.

entries.name: Mirror (5 GP)
entries: A handheld steel Mirror is useful for personal cosmetics but also for peeking around corners and reflecting light as a signal.

entries.name: Net (1 GP)
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action, you can replace one of your attacks with throwing a Net. Target a creature you can see within 15 feet of yourself. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw ({@dc 8} plus your Dexterity modifier and Proficiency Bonus) or have the {@condition Restrained|srd52} condition until it escapes. The target succeeds automatically if it is Huge or larger.

To escape, the target or a creature within 5 feet of it must take an action to make a {@dc 10} Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check, freeing the Restrained creature on a success. Destroying the Net (AC 10; 5 HP; Immunity to Bludgeoning, Poison, and Psychic damage) also frees the target, ending the effect.

entries.name: Oil (1 SP)
entries: You can douse a creature, object, or space with Oil or use it as fuel, as detailed below.

entries.name: Dousing a Creature or an Object
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action, you can replace one of your attacks with throwing an Oil flask. Target one creature or object within 20 feet of yourself. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw ({@dc 8} plus your Dexterity modifier and Proficiency Bonus) or be covered in oil. If the target takes Fire damage before the oil dries (after 1 minute), the target takes an extra 5 Fire damage from burning oil.

entries.name: Dousing a Space
entries: You can take the {@action Utilize|srd52} action to pour an Oil flask on level ground to cover a 5-foot-square area within 5 feet of yourself. If lit, the oil burns until the end of the turn 2 rounds from when the oil was lit (or 12 seconds) and deals 5 Fire damage to any creature that enters the area or ends its turn there. A creature can take this damage only once per turn.

entries.name: Fuel
entries: Oil serves as fuel for Lamps and Lanterns. Once lit, a flask of Oil burns for 6 hours in a Lamp or Lantern. That duration doesn't need to be consecutive; you can extinguish the burning Oil (as a {@action Utilize|srd52} action) and rekindle it again until it has burned for a total of 6 hours.

entries.name: Paper (2 SP)
entries: One sheet of Paper can hold about 250 handwritten words.

entries.name: Parchment (1 SP)
entries: One sheet of Parchment can hold about 250 handwritten words.

entries.name: Perfume (5 GP)
entries: Perfume comes in a 4-ounce vial. For 1 hour after applying Perfume to yourself, you have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on Charisma ({@skill Persuasion|srd52}) checks made to influence an {@variantrule Indifferent [Attitude]|srd52|Indifferent} Humanoid within 5 feet of yourself.

entries.name: Poison, Basic (100 GP)
entries: As a Bonus Action, you can use a vial of Basic Poison to coat one weapon or up to three pieces of ammunition. A creature that takes Piercing or Slashing damage from the poisoned weapon or ammunition takes an extra {@dice 1d4} Poison damage. Once applied, the poison retains potency for 1 minute or until its damage is dealt, whichever comes first.

entries.name: Pole (5 CP)
entries: A Pole is 10 feet long. You can use it to touch something up to 10 feet away. If you must make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check as part of a {@variantrule High Jump|srd52|High} or {@variantrule Long Jump|srd52}, you can use the Pole to vault, giving yourself {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on the check.

entries.name: Pot, Iron (2 GP)
entries: An Iron Pot holds up to 1 gallon.

entries.name: Potion of Healing (50 GP)
entries: This potion is a magic item. As a Bonus Action, you can drink it or administer it to another creature within 5 feet of yourself. The creature that drinks the magical red fluid in this vial regains {@dice 2d4 + 2} Hit Points.

entries.name: Pouch (5 SP)
entries: A Pouch holds up to 6 pounds within one-fifth of a cubic foot.

entries.name: Priest's Pack (33 GP)
entries: A Priest's Pack contains the following items: {@item Backpack|srd52}, {@item Blanket|srd52}, {@item Holy Water|srd52}, {@item Lamp|srd52}, 7 days of {@item Rations|srd52}, {@item Robe|srd52}, and {@item Tinderbox|srd52}.

entries.name: Quiver (1 GP)
entries: A Quiver holds up to 20 {@item Arrows (20)|srd52|Arrows}.

entries.name: Ram, Portable (4 GP)
entries: You can use a Portable Ram to break down doors. When doing so, you gain a +4 bonus to the Strength check. One other character can help you use the ram, giving you {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on this check.

entries.name: Rations (5 SP)
entries: Rations consist of travel-ready food, including jerky, dried fruit, hardtack, and nuts. See "{@hazard Malnutrition|srd52}" in the {@book rules glossary|srd52|10|Malnutrition [Hazard]} for the risks of not eating.

entries.name: Robe (1 GP)
entries: A Robe has vocational or ceremonial significance. Some events and locations admit only people wearing a Robe bearing certain colors or symbols.

entries.name: Rope (1 GP)
entries: As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can tie a knot with Rope if you succeed on a {@dc 10} Dexterity ({@skill Sleight of Hand|srd52}) check. The Rope can be burst with a successful {@dc 20} Strength ({@skill Athletics|srd52}) check.

You can bind an unwilling creature with the Rope only if the creature has the {@condition Grappled|srd52}, {@condition Incapacitated|srd52}, or {@condition Restrained|srd52} condition. If the creature's legs are bound, the creature has the Restrained condition until it escapes. Escaping the Rope requires the creature to make a successful {@dc 15} Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|srd52}) check as an action.

entries.name: Sack (1 CP)
entries: A Sack holds up to 30 pounds within 1 cubic foot.

entries.name: Scholar's Pack (40 GP)
entries: A Scholar's Pack contains the following items: {@item Backpack|srd52}, {@item Book|srd52}, {@item Ink|srd52}, {@item Ink Pen|srd52}, {@item Lamp|srd52}, 10 flasks of {@item Oil|srd52}, 10 sheets of {@item Parchment|srd52}, and {@item Tinderbox|srd52}.

entries.name: Shovel (2 GP)
entries: Working for 1 hour, you can use a Shovel to dig a hole that is 5 feet on each side in soil or similar material.

entries.name: Signal Whistle (5 CP)
entries: When blown as a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, a Signal Whistle produces a sound that can be heard up to 600 feet away.

entries.name: Spell Scroll (Cantrip, 30 GP Level 1, 50 GP)
entries: A {@i Spell Scroll} (Cantrip) or {@i Spell Scroll} (Level 1) is a magic item that bears the words of a cantrip or level 1 spell, respectively, determined by the scroll's creator. If the spell is on your class's spell list, you can read the scroll and cast the spell using its normal casting time and without providing any Material components.
If the spell requires a saving throw or an attack roll, the spell save DC is 13, and the attack bonus is +5. The scroll disintegrates when the casting is completed.

entries.name: Spikes, Iron (1 GP)
entries: Iron Spikes come in bundles of ten. As a {@action Utilize|srd52} action, you can use a blunt object, such as a {@item Light Hammer|srd52}, to hammer a spike into wood, earth, or a similar material. You can do so to jam a door shut or to then tie a {@item Rope|srd52} or {@item Chain|srd52} to the Spike.

entries.name: Spyglass (1,000 GP)
entries: Objects viewed through a Spyglass are magnified to twice their size.

entries.name: String (1 SP)
entries: String is 10 feet long. You can tie a knot in it as a {@action Utilize|srd52} action.

entries.name: Tent (2 GP)
entries: A Tent sleeps up to two Small or Medium creatures.

entries.name: Tinderbox (5 SP)
entries: A Tinderbox is a small container holding flint, fire steel, and tinder (usually dry cloth soaked in light oil) used to kindle a fire. Using it to light a {@item Candle|srd52}, {@item Lamp|srd52}, Lantern, or {@item Torch|srd52}—or anything else with exposed fuel—takes a Bonus Action. Lighting any other fire takes 1 minute.

entries.name: Torch (1 CP)
entries: A Torch burns for 1 hour, casting {@variantrule Bright Light|srd52} in a 20-foot radius and {@variantrule Dim Light|srd52} for an additional 20 feet. When you take the {@action Attack|srd52} action, you can attack with the Torch, using it as a Simple Melee weapon. On a hit, the target takes 1 Fire damage.

entries.name: Vial (1 GP)
entries: A Vial holds up to 4 ounces.

entries.name: Waterskin (2 SP)
entries: A Waterskin holds up to 4 pints. If you don't drink sufficient water, you risk {@hazard dehydration|srd52}.

entries.name: Mounts and Vehicles
entries: A mount can help you move more quickly through the wilderness, but its primary purpose is to carry gear that would otherwise slow you down. The {@book Mounts and Other Animals table|srd52|6|Mounts and Other Animals} shows each animal's carrying capacity. See {@book appendix B|srd52|9} for the animals' stat blocks.

entries.name: Mounts and Cargo
entries: An animal pulling a carriage, cart, chariot, sled, or wagon can move weight up to five times its base carrying capacity, including the weight of the vehicle. If multiple animals pull the same vehicle, add their carrying capacities together.

entries.name: Barding
entries: Barding is armor designed for a mount. Any type of armor on the {@book Armor table|srd52|6|Armor} in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" can be purchased as barding. The cost is four times the normal cost, and it weighs twice as much.

entries.name: Saddles
entries: A saddle comes with a bit, a bridle, reins, and any other equipment needed to use the saddle. A Military Saddle gives {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on any ability check you make to remain mounted. An Exotic Saddle is required for riding an aquatic or a flying mount.

entries.name: Large Vehicles
entries: The Airborne and Waterborne Vehicles table provides statistics for various types of large vehicles. The following notes apply.

entries.name: Speed
entries: A ship sailing against a strong wind moves at half speed. In a dead calm (no wind), waterborne ships can't move under sail and must be rowed. Keelboats and Rowboats are used on lakes and rivers. If going downstream, add the speed of the current (typically 3 miles per hour) to the speed of the vehicle. These vehicles can't be rowed against any significant current, but they can be pulled upstream by draft animals on the shores. A Rowboat can be carried and weighs 100 pounds.

entries.name: Crew
entries: A ship larger than a Keelboat or Rowboat needs a crew of skilled hirelings (see "{@book Hirelings|srd52|6|Hirelings}" later in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}") to function. The minimum number of skilled hirelings needed to crew a ship depends on the type of ship, as shown in the table.

entries.name: Passengers
entries: The table lists the number of Small and Medium passengers the ship can accommodate using hammocks. A ship outfitted with private accommodations can carry one-fifth as many passengers. A passenger usually pays 5 SP per day for a hammock, but prices can vary from ship to ship. A small private cabin usually costs 2 GP per day.

entries.name: Damage Threshold
entries: If a vehicle has a {@variantrule damage threshold|srd52}, it's noted in the table.

entries.name: Ship Repair
entries: Repairs to a damaged ship can be made while the vessel is berthed. Repairing 1 Hit Point of damage requires 1 day and costs 20 GP for materials and labor. If the repairs are made in a location where supplies and skilled labor are abundant, such as a city shipyard, the repair time and cost are halved.

entries.name: Lifestyle Expenses
entries: Lifestyle expenses summarize the cost of living in a fantasy world. They cover lodging, food, equipment maintenance, and other necessities.
At the start of each week or month (GM's choice), choose a lifestyle below—Wretched, Squalid, Poor, Modest, Comfortable, Wealthy, or Aristocratic—and pay the price to sustain that lifestyle.
Lifestyles have no inherent consequences, but the GM might take them into account when determining risks or how others perceive your character.

entries.name: Wretched (Free)
entries: You survive via chance and charity. You're often exposed to natural dangers as a result of sleeping outside.

entries.name: Squalid (1 SP per Day)
entries: You spend the bare minimum for your necessities. You might be exposed to unhealthy conditions and opportunistic criminals.

entries.name: Poor (2 SP per Day)
entries: You spend frugally for your necessities.

entries.name: Modest (1 GP per Day)
entries: You support yourself at an average level.

entries.name: Comfortable (2 GP per Day)
entries: You spend modestly for your necessities and enjoy a few luxuries.

entries.name: Wealthy (4 GP per Day)
entries: You're accustomed to the finer things in life and might have servants.

entries.name: Aristocratic (10 GP per Day)
entries: You pay for the best and might have a staff that supports your lifestyle. Others notice your wealth and might encourage you to share it, either legally or otherwise.

entries.name: Food, Drink, and Lodging
entries: The Food, Drink, and Lodging table gives prices for food and a single night's lodging. Prices for daily lodging and meals are included in your lifestyle's expenses.

entries.name: Hirelings
entries: Skilled hirelings include anyone hired to perform a service that involves a proficiency (including weapon, tool, or skill): a mercenary, an artisan, a scribe, or the like. The pay shown on the Hirelings table is a minimum; some expert hirelings require more pay. Untrained hirelings are hired for work that requires no particular proficiencies; they include laborers and porters.

entries.name: Spellcasting
entries: Most settlements contain individuals who are willing to cast spells in exchange for payment. If a spell has expensive components, add the cost of those components to the cost listed in the Spellcasting Services table. The higher the level of a desired spell, the harder it is to find someone to cast it.

entries.name: Magic Items
entries: Adventures hold the promise—but not a guarantee—of finding magic items. Hundreds of magic items are detailed in "{@book Magic Items|srd52|11}" later in this document. Here's what you need to know about using magic items.

entries.name: Identifying a Magic Item
entries: Some magic items are indistinguishable from their nonmagical counterparts, while others are conspicuously magical. Handling a magic item is enough to give you a sense that it is extraordinary, but learning a magic item's properties isn't automatic.

The {@spell Identify|srd52} spell is the fastest way to reveal an item's properties. Alternatively, you can focus on one magic item during a {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52} while being in physical contact with the item. At the end of the rest, you learn its properties and how to use them (but not any curse the item might bear).

Sometimes a magic item carries a clue to its properties. The command word to activate a ring might be etched inside the band, or a feathered design might hint that it's a {@item Ring of Feather Falling|srd52}.

Wearing or experimenting with an item can also offer hints about its properties. In the specific case of Potions, a little taste is enough to tell the taster what a potion does. Other items might require more experimentation. For example, if your character puts on a {@item Ring of Swimming|srd52}, the GM might say, "Your movement feels strangely fluid." Perhaps you then dive into a river to see what happens. The GM would then say you swim unexpectedly well.

entries.name: Attunement
entries: Some magic items require a creature to form a bond—called Attunement—with them before the creature can use an item's magical properties. Without becoming attuned to an item that requires Attunement, you gain only its nonmagical benefits unless its description states otherwise. For example, a magic Shield that requires Attunement provides the benefits of a normal Shield if you aren't attuned to it, but none of its magical properties.

entries.name: Attune during a Short Rest
entries: Attuning to an item requires you to spend a {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52} focused on only that item while being in physical contact with it (this can't be the same Short Rest used to learn the item's properties). This focus can take the form of weapon practice (for a Weapon), meditation (for a Wand), or some other appropriate activity. If the Short Rest is interrupted, the Attunement attempt fails. Otherwise, at the end of the Short Rest, you're attuned to the magic item and can access its full magical capabilities.

entries.name: No More Than Three Items
entries: You can be attuned to no more than three magic items at a time. Any attempt to attune to a fourth item fails; you must end your Attunement to an item first. Additionally, you can't attune to more than one copy of an item. For example, you can't attune to more than one {@item Ring of Protection|srd52} at a time.

entries.name: Ending Attunement
entries: Your Attunement to an item ends if you no longer satisfy the prerequisites for Attunement, if the item has been more than 100 feet away for at least 24 hours, if you die, or if another creature attunes to the item. You can also voluntarily end Attunement by spending another {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52} focused on the item unless the item is cursed.

entries.name: Wearing and Wielding Items
entries: Using a magic item's properties might mean wearing or wielding it. A magic item meant to be worn must be donned in the intended fashion: boots go on feet, gloves on hands, hats and helmets on a head, and rings on a finger. Magic armor must be donned, a Shield strapped to the arm, a cloak fastened about the shoulders. A weapon must be held.
In most cases, a magic item that's meant to be worn can fit a creature regardless of size or build. Magic garments are made to be easily adjustable, or they magically adjust themselves to the wearer.

entries.name: Multiple Items of the Same Kind
entries: You can't wear more than one of certain magic items. You can't normally wear more than one pair of footwear, one pair of gloves or gauntlets, one pair of bracers, one suit of armor, one item of headwear, or one cloak. The GM might make exceptions.

entries.name: Paired Items
entries: Items that come in pairs—such as boots, bracers, gauntlets, and gloves—impart their benefits only if both items of the pair are worn. For example, a character wearing a {@item Boots of Striding and Springing|srd52|Boot of Striding and Springing} on one foot and a {@item Boots of Elvenkind|srd52|Boot of Elvenkind} on the other foot gains no benefit from either.

entries.name: Crafting Nonmagical Items
entries: To craft a nonmagical item, you need tools, raw materials, and time, each of which is detailed below. If you meet the requirements, you make the item, and you can use it or sell it at its normal price.

entries.name: Tools
entries: The "{@book Tools|srd52|6|Tools}" section of "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" lists which tools are required to make certain items. The GM assigns required tools for items not listed there.
You must use the required tool to make an item and have proficiency with that tool. Anyone who helps you must also have proficiency with it.

entries.name: Raw Materials
entries: To make an item, you need raw materials worth half its purchase cost (round down). For example, you need 750 GP of raw materials to make Plate Armor, which sells for 1,500 GP. The GM determines whether appropriate raw materials are available.

entries.name: Time
entries: To determine how many days (working 8 hours a day) it takes to make an item, divide its purchase cost in GP by 10 (round a fraction up to a day). For example, you need 5 days to make a Heavy Crossbow, which sells for 50 GP.
If an item requires multiple days, the days needn't be consecutive.

Characters can combine their efforts to shorten the crafting time. Divide the time needed to create an item by the number of characters working on it. Normally, only one other character can assist you, but the GM might allow more assistants.

entries.name: Brewing Potions of Healing
entries: A character who has proficiency with the Herbalism Kit can create a {@item Potion of Healing|srd52}. Doing so requires using that kit and 25 GP of raw material over the course of 1 day (8 hours of work).

entries.name: Scribing Spell Scrolls
entries: A spellcaster can transfer a spell to a scroll and create a {@item Spell Scroll|srd52}, using the rules below.

entries.name: Time and Cost
entries: Scribing a scroll takes an amount of time and money based on the level of the spell, as shown in the {@book Spell Scroll Costs table|srd52|6|Spell Scroll Costs}. For each day of inscription, you must work for 8 hours. If a scroll requires multiple days, those days needn't be consecutive.

entries.name: Prerequisites for the Scribe
entries: To scribe a scroll, you must have proficiency in the {@skill Arcana|srd52} skill or with {@item Calligrapher's Supplies|srd52} and have the spell prepared on each day of the inscription. You must also have at hand any Material components required by the spell; if the spell consumes its Material components, they are consumed only when you complete the scroll. The scroll's spell uses your spell save DC and spell attack bonus.

entries.name: Cantrips
entries: If the scribed spell is a cantrip, the version on the scroll works as if the caster were your level.

entries.name: Gaining Spells
entries: Before you can cast a spell, you must have the spell prepared in your mind or have access to the spell from a magic item, such as a {@item Spell Scroll|srd52}. Your features specify which spells you have access to, if any; whether you always have certain spells prepared; and whether you can change the list of spells you have prepared.

entries.name: Preparing Spells
entries: If you have a list of level 1+ spells you prepare, your spellcasting feature specifies when you can change the list and the number of spells you can change, as summarized in the Spell Preparation by Class table.
Most spellcasting monsters don't change their lists of prepared spells, but the GM is free to alter them.

entries.name: Always-Prepared Spells
entries: Certain features might give you a spell that you always have prepared. If you also have a list of prepared spells that you can change, a spell that you always have prepared doesn't count against the number of spells on that list.

entries.name: Casting in Armor
entries: You must have training with any armor you are wearing to cast spells while wearing it. You are otherwise too hampered by the armor for spellcasting.

entries.name: Casting Spells
entries: Each spell description has a series of entries that provide the details needed to cast the spell. The following sections explain each of those entries, which follow a spell's name.

entries.name: Spell Level
entries: Every spell has a level from 0 to 9, which is indicated in a spell's description. A spell's level is an indicator of how powerful it is. Cantrips—simple spells that can be cast almost by rote—are level 0. The rules for each spellcasting class say when its members gain access to spells of certain levels.

entries.name: Spell Slots
entries: Spellcasting is taxing, so a spellcaster can cast only a limited number of level 1+ spells before resting. Spell slots are the main way a spellcaster's magical potential is represented. Each spellcasting class gives its members a limited number of spell slots of certain spell levels. For example, a level 3 Wizard has four level 1 spell slots and two level 2 slots.

When you cast a spell, you expend a slot of that spell's level or higher, effectively "filling" a slot with the spell. Imagine a spell slot is a groove of a certain size—small for a level 1 slot and larger for a higher-level spell. A level 1 spell fits into a slot of any size, but a level 2 spell fits only into a slot that's at least level 2. So when a level 3 Wizard casts {@spell Magic Missile|srd52}, a level 1 spell, that Wizard spends one of four level 1 slots and has three remaining.
Finishing a {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} restores any expended spell slots.

entries.name: Casting without Slots
entries: There are several ways to cast a spell without expending a spell slot:

items.name: Cantrips
items.entry: A cantrip is cast without a spell slot.

items.name: Rituals
items.entry: Certain spells have the Ritual tag in the Casting Time entry. Such a spell can be cast following the normal rules for spellcasting, or it can be cast as a Ritual. The Ritual version of a spell takes 10 minutes longer to cast than normal, but it doesn't expend a spell slot. To cast a spell as a Ritual, a spellcaster must have it prepared.

items.name: Special Abilities
items.entry: Some characters and monsters have special abilities that allow them to cast specific spells without a spell slot. This casting is usually limited in another way, such as being able to cast the spell a limited number of times per day.

items.name: Magic Items
items.entry: {@item Spell Scroll|srd52|Spell Scrolls} and some other magic items contain spells that can be cast without a spell slot. The description of such an item specifies how many times a spell can be cast from it.

entries.name: Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot
entries: When a spellcaster casts a spell using a slot that is of a higher level than the spell, the spell takes on the higher level for that casting. For instance, if a Wizard casts {@spell Magic Missile|srd52} using a level 2 slot, that {@i Magic Missile} is level 2. Effectively, the spell expands to fill the slot it is put into.
Some spells, such as {@spell Magic Missile|srd52} and {@spell Cure Wounds|srd52}, have more powerful effects when cast at a higher level, as detailed in a spell's description.

entries.name: School of Magic
entries: Each spell belongs to a school of magic. The schools are listed in the Schools of Magic table. These categories help describe spells but have no rules of their own, although some other rules refer to them.

entries.caption: Schools of Magic
rows: Channels energy to create effects that are often destructive

entries.name: Class Spell Lists
entries: If a spell is on a class's spell list, the class's name appears in parentheses after the spell's school of magic. Some features add a spell to a character's spell list even if the character isn't a member of a class in the parentheses.

entries.name: Casting Time
entries: Most spells require the {@action Magic|srd52} action to cast, but some spells require a Bonus Action, a Reaction, or 1 minute or more. A spell's Casting Time entry specifies which of those is required.

entries.name: One Spell with a Spell Slot per Turn
entries: On a turn, you can expend only one spell slot to cast a spell. This rule means you can't, for example, cast a spell with a spell slot using the {@action Magic|srd52} action and another one using a Bonus Action on the same turn.

entries.name: Reaction and Bonus Action Triggers
entries: A spell that has a casting time of a Reaction is cast in response to a trigger that is defined in the spell's Casting Time entry. Some spells that have a casting time of a Bonus Action are also cast in response to a trigger defined in the spell.

entries.name: Longer Casting Times
entries: Certain spells—including a spell cast as a {@variantrule Ritual|srd52}—require more time to cast: minutes or even hours. While you cast a spell with a casting time of 1 minute or more, you must take the {@action Magic|srd52} action on each of your turns, and you must maintain Concentration (see "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}") while you do so. If your Concentration is broken, the spell fails, but you don't expend a spell slot. To cast the spell again, you must start over.

entries.name: Range
entries: A spell's range indicates how far from the spellcaster the spell's effect can originate, and the spell's description specifies which part of the effect is limited by the range.
A range usually takes one of the following forms:

items.name: Distance
items.entry: The range is expressed in feet.

items.name: Touch
items.entry: The spell's effect originates on something, as defined by the spell, that the spellcaster must touch within their reach.

items.name: Self
items.entry: The spell is cast on the spellcaster or emanates from them, as specified in the spell.

entries: If a spell has movable effects, they aren't restricted by its range unless the spell's description says otherwise.

entries.name: Components
entries: A spell's components are physical requirements the spellcaster must meet to cast the spell. Each spell's description indicates whether it requires Verbal (V), Somatic (S), or Material (M) components. If the spellcaster can't provide one or more of a spell's components, the spellcaster can't cast the spell.

entries.name: Verbal (V)
entries: A Verbal component is the chanting of esoteric words that sound like nonsense to the uninitiated. The words must be uttered in a normal speaking voice. The words themselves aren't the source of the spell's power; rather, the particular combination of sounds, with specific pitch and resonance, sets the threads of magic in motion. Thus, a creature who is gagged or in an area of magical silence can't cast a spell with a Verbal component.

entries.name: Somatic (S)
entries: A Somatic component is a forceful gesticulation or an intricate set of gestures. A spellcaster must use at least one of their hands to perform these movements.

entries.name: Material (M)
entries: A Material component is a particular material used in a spell's casting, as specified in parentheses in the Components entry. These materials aren't consumed by the spell unless the spell's description states otherwise. The spellcaster must have a hand free to access them, but it can be the same hand used to perform Somatic components, if any.

If a spell doesn't consume its materials and doesn't specify a cost for them, a spellcaster can use a {@item Component Pouch|srd52} (see {@book Equipment|srd52|6|Component Pouch (25 GP)}) instead of providing the materials specified in the spell, or the spellcaster can substitute a {@variantrule Spellcasting Focus|srd52} if the caster has a feature that allows that substitution. To use a Component Pouch, you must have a hand free to reach into it, and to use a {@variantrule Spellcasting Focus|srd52}, you must hold it unless its description says otherwise (see {@book Equipment|srd52|6} for descriptions).

entries.name: Duration
entries: A spell's duration is the length of time the spell persists after it is cast. A duration typically takes one of the following forms:

items.name: Concentration
items.entry: A duration that requires Concentration follows the Concentration rules (see "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}").

items.name: Instantaneous
items.entry: An instantaneous duration means the spell's magic appears only for a moment and then disappears.

items.name: Time Span
items.entry: A duration that provides a time span specifies how long the spell lasts in rounds, minutes, hours, or the like. For example, a Duration entry might say "1 minute," meaning the spell ends after 1 minute has passed. While a time-span spell that you cast is ongoing, you can dismiss it (no action required) if you don't have the {@condition Incapacitated|srd52} condition.

entries.name: Effects
entries: The effects of a spell are detailed after its duration entry. Those details present exactly what the spell does, which ignores mundane physical laws; any outcomes beyond those effects are under the GM's purview. Whatever the effects, they typically deal with targets, saving throws, attack rolls, or all three, each of which is detailed below.

entries.name: Targets
entries: A typical spell requires the caster to pick one or more targets to be affected by the spell's magic. A spell's description says whether the spell targets creatures, objects, or something else.

entries.name: A Clear Path to the Target
entries: To target something with a spell, a caster must have a clear path to it, so it can't be behind {@variantrule Cover|srd52|Total Cover}.

entries.name: Targeting Yourself
entries: If a spell targets a creature of your choice, you can choose yourself unless the creature must be {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|srd52|Hostile} or specifically a creature other than you.

entries.name: Areas of Effect
entries: Some spells, such as {@spell Thunderwave|srd52}, cover an area called an {@variantrule area of effect|srd52}, which is defined in "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}". The area determines what the spell targets. The description of a spell specifies whether it has an area of effect, which is typically one of these shapes: {@variantrule Cone [Area of Effect]|srd52|Cone}, {@variantrule Cube [Area of Effect]|srd52|Cube}, {@variantrule Cylinder [Area of Effect]|srd52|Cylinder}, {@variantrule Emanation [Area of Effect]|srd52|Emanation}, {@variantrule Line [Area of Effect]|srd52|Line}, or {@variantrule Sphere [Area of Effect]|srd52|Sphere}.

entries.name: Awareness of Being Targeted
entries: Unless a spell has a perceptible effect, a creature doesn't know it was targeted by the spell. An effect like lightning is obvious, but a more subtle effect, such as an attempt to read thoughts, goes unnoticed unless a spell's description says otherwise.

entries.name: Invalid Targets
entries: If you cast a spell on someone or something that can't be affected by it, nothing happens to that target, but if you used a spell slot to cast the spell, the slot is still expended.

If the spell normally has no effect on a target that succeeds on a saving throw, the invalid target appears to have succeeded on its saving throw, even though it didn't attempt one (giving no hint that the creature is an invalid target). Otherwise, you perceive that the spell did nothing to the target.

entries.name: Saving Throws
entries: Many spells specify that a target makes a saving throw to avoid some or all of a spell's effects. The spell specifies the ability that the target uses for the save and what happens on a success or failure. Here's how to calculate the DC for your spells:

entries.name: Attack Rolls
entries: Some spells require the caster to make an attack roll to determine whether the spell hits a target. Here's how to calculate the attack modifier for your spells:

entries.name: Combining Spell Effects
entries: The effects of different spells add together while their durations overlap. In contrast, the effects of the same spell cast multiple times don't combine. Instead, the most potent effect—such as the highest bonus—from those castings applies while their durations overlap. The most recent effect applies if the castings are equally potent and their durations overlap. For example, if two Clerics cast {@spell Bless|srd52} on the same target, that target gains the spell's benefit only once; the target doesn't receive two bonus dice. But if the durations of the spells overlap, the effect continues until the duration of the second {@i Bless} ends.

entries.name: Identifying an Ongoing Spell
entries: You can try to identify a non-instantaneous spell by its observable effects if its duration is ongoing. To identify it, you must take the {@action Study|srd52} action and succeed on a {@dc 15} Intelligence ({@skill Arcana|srd52}) check.

entries.name: Glossary Conventions
entries: The glossary uses the following conventions:

items.name: Tags in Brackets
items.entry: Some entries have a tag in brackets after the entry's name, as in "Attack [Action]." A tag—Action, Area of Effect, Attitude, Condition, or Hazard—indicates that a rule is part of a family of rules. The tags also have glossary entries.

items.name: "You"
items.entry: The game's rules—in this glossary and elsewhere—often talk about something happening to you in the game world. That "you" refers to the creature or object that the rule applies to in a particular moment of play. For example, the "you" in the {@condition Prone|srd52} condition is a creature that currently has that condition.

items.name: "See Also"
items.entry: Some glossary entries include a See also section that points to other entries in the glossary, to other parts of this document, or both.

items.name: No Obsolete Terms
items.entry: The glossary contains definitions of current rules terms only. If you're looking for a term from an earlier version of the fifth edition rules, consult the index.

items.name: Abbreviations
