items.entry: The abbreviations listed below appear in this glossary and elsewhere in the rules.

entries.name: Rules Definitions
entries: Here are definitions of various rules.

entries.name: Travel Pace
entries: A group of characters can travel overland at a Normal, Fast, or Slow pace, as described in "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}". During any journey stage, the predominant terrain determines the characters' maximum travel pace, as shown in the Maximum Pace column of the Travel Terrain table. Certain factors can affect a group's travel pace.

entries.name: Good Roads
entries: The presence of a good road increases the group's maximum pace by one step (from Slow to Normal or from Normal to Fast).

entries.name: Slower Travelers
entries: The group must move at a Slow pace if any group member's Speed is reduced to half or less of normal.

entries.name: Extended Travel
entries: Characters can push themselves to travel for more than 8 hours per day, at the risk of tiring. At the end of each additional hour of travel beyond 8 hours, each character must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or gain 1 {@condition Exhaustion|srd52} level. The DC is 10 plus 1 for each hour past 8 hours.

entries.name: Special Movement
entries: If a party can travel at a high Speed for an extended time, as with a spell such as {@spell Wind Walk|srd52} or a magic item such as a {@item Carpet of Flying|srd52}, translate the party's Speed into travel rates using these rules:

entries.name: Miles per day (Normal pace)
entries.text: Miles per hour × number of hours traveled (typically 8)

entries: If the characters are flying or their special movement allows them to ignore {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|srd52}, they can move at a Fast pace regardless of the terrain.

entries.name: Vehicles
entries: Characters traveling in a vehicle use the vehicle's speed in miles per hour (as shown in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}") to determine their rate of travel, and they don't choose a travel pace.

entries.caption: Travel Terrain
footnotes: *Appropriate equipment (such as skis) is necessary to keep up a Fast pace in Arctic terrain.
†Characters' rate of travel while waterborne depends on the vehicle carrying them; see "Vehicles."

entries.name: Creating a Background
entries: A character's background represents what the character did prior to becoming an adventurer. Creating a unique background or customizing an existing one can reflect the particular theme of your campaign or elements of your world. You can also create a background to help a player craft the story they have in mind for their character.
This section describes, step by step, how you can create backgrounds tailored for your world and the heroes in it.

entries.name: 1: Choose Abilities
entries: Choose three abilities that seem appropriate for the background:

items.name: Strength or Dexterity
items.entry: These abilities are ideal for a background involving physical exertion.

items.name: Constitution
items.entry: This ability is ideal for a background that involves endurance or long hours of activity.

items.name: Intelligence or Wisdom
items.entry: One or both abilities are ideal for a background that focuses on cerebral or spiritual matters.

items.name: Charisma
items.entry: This ability is ideal for a background that involves performance or social interaction.

entries.name: 2: Choose a Feat
entries: Choose one feat from the Origin category. See "{@book Origin Feats|srd52|5|Origin Feats}" for examples of Origin feats.

entries.name: 3: Choose Skill Proficiencies
entries: Choose two skills appropriate for the background. There needn't be a relationship between the skill proficiencies a background grants and the ability scores it increases.

entries.name: 4: Choose a Tool Proficiency
entries: Choose one tool used in the practice of the background or often associated with it.

entries.name: 5: Choose Equipment
entries: Assemble a package of equipment worth 50 GP (including unspent gold). Don't include Martial weapons or armor, as characters get them from their class choices.

entries.name: Curses and Magical Contagions
entries: A curse is a magical burden that lasts for a specified time or until it is ended by some means. A magical contagion is an adverse effect of magical origin that is contagious by definition.
The following sections discuss curses and magical contagions in detail.

entries.name: Curses
entries: Every curse has rules that govern it. A curse typically takes one of the forms detailed below.

entries.name: Bestow Curse
entries: The simplest curses are created by the {@spell Bestow Curse|srd52} spell. The effects of such curses are limited and can be ended by the {@spell Remove Curse|srd52} spell.

{@i Bestow Curse} provides useful benchmarks for gauging the potency of other curses. A curse that lasts for 1 minute equates to a level 3 spell, while one that lasts until dispelled equates to a level 9 spell.

entries.name: Cursed Creatures
entries: Some monsters are associated with curses, whether as part of their origins or due to their ability to spread curses—werewolves being a prime example.

You decide how a spell like {@spell Remove Curse|srd52} affects a creature with accursed origins. For example, you might decide that a mummy was created through a curse and it can be destroyed permanently only by casting {@i Remove Curse} on its corpse.

entries.name: Cursed Magic Items
entries: Cursed magic items are created deliberately or originate as the result of supernatural events. Such items are detailed in "{@book Magic Items|srd52|11}".

entries.name: Narrative Curses
entries: A curse might manifest during an adventure when a creature's violation of a taboo warrants supernatural punishment, such as breaking a vow, defiling a tomb, or murdering an innocent. Such a curse can have any effects you design, or it might be a customized version of another type of curse discussed in this section.

A creature affected by such a curse should know why they're being punished and be able to learn how to end their curse, likely by symbolically righting the wrong they committed. How a spell like {@spell Remove Curse|srd52} affects a curse that's part of your adventure is up to you—the spell might merely suppress the effects of the curse for a time. Regardless, narrative curses should feel like rare, potent magic rooted in the lore of your campaign.

entries.name: Environmental Curses
entries: Some locations are so suffused with evil that anyone who lingers there is burdened with a curse. Demonic Possession is one example of an environmental curse.

entries.name: Demonic Possession
entries: Demonic Possession arises from the chaos and evil of the {@book Abyss|srd52|5|Abyss} and commonly besets creatures that interact with demonic objects or linger in desecrated locations, where demonic spirits await victims.

A creature that becomes the target of Demonic Possession must succeed on a {@dc 15} Charisma saving throw or be possessed by a bodiless demonic entity. Whenever the possessed creature rolls a 1 on a {@variantrule D20 Test|srd52}, the demonic entity takes control of the creature and determines the creature's behavior thereafter. At the end of each of the possessed creature's later turns, the creature makes a {@dc 15} Charisma saving throw, regaining control of itself on a success.

After finishing a Long Rest, a creature with Demonic Possession makes a {@dc 15} Charisma saving throw. On a successful save, the effect ends on the creature. A {@spell Dispel Evil and Good|srd52} spell or any magic that removes a curse also ends the effect on it.

entries.name: Magical Contagions
entries: Alchemists, potion brewers, and areas of wild magic are credited with creating the first magical contagions. An outbreak of such a contagion can form the basis of an adventure as characters search for a cure and try to stop the contagion's spread.

entries.name: Rest and Recuperation
entries: If a creature infected with a magical contagion spends 3 days recuperating, engaging in no activities that would interrupt a Long Rest, the creature makes a {@dc 15} Constitution saving throw at the end of the recuperation period. On a successful save, the creature has {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on saving throws to fight off the magical contagion for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Example Contagions
entries: The following examples show how magical contagions can work. Feel free to alter the saving throw DCs, effects, and other characteristics of these contagions to suit your campaign.

entries.name: Fear and Mental Stress
entries: Due to the nature of their vocation, adventurers tend to be less susceptible to fear and mental stress than common folk. Whereas a farmer might flee in terror from a bear or an apparition, adventurers are made of sterner stuff. That said, certain creatures and game effects can terrify or fray the mind of even the most stalwart adventurer.
If you plan to use any of these rules, discuss them with your players at the start of the campaign.

entries.name: Fear Effects
entries: Whenever the characters encounter something that is supernaturally frightful, use the {@condition Frightened|srd52} condition as the baseline effect. Fear effects typically require a Wisdom saving throw, with a save DC set based on how terrifying the situation is. The Sample Fear DCs table provides some examples.

entries.caption: Sample Fear DCs
rows: When the characters open a sarcophagus, a harmless yet terrifying apparition appears.
A character triggers a magical trap that creates an illusory manifestation of that character's worst fears, visible only to that character.
A portal to the Abyss opens, revealing a nightmarish realm of torment and slaughter.

entries: Typically, a {@condition Frightened|srd52} creature repeats the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success.
At your discretion, a Frightened creature might be subject to other effects as long as the Frightened condition lasts. Consider these examples:

items: The Frightened creature must take the {@action Dash|srd52} action on each of its turns and uses its movement to get farther away from the source of its fear.
Attack rolls against the Frightened creature have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52}.
The Frightened creature can do only one of the following on each of its turns: move, take an action, or take a Bonus Action.

entries.name: Mental Stress Effects
entries: When a character is subjected to an effect that causes intense mental stress, Psychic damage is the best way to emulate that effect.

The Sample Mental Stress Effects table provides a few examples of such effects, with suggested saving throw DCs and damage. Mental stress can usually be resisted with a successful Wisdom save, but sometimes an Intelligence or Charisma save is more appropriate. On a successful save, a character might take half as much damage instead of no damage, at your discretion.

entries.caption: Sample Mental Stress Effects
rows: A character ingests a hallucinogenic substance that distorts the character's perception of reality.
A character touches a fiendish idol that tears at the character's mind, threatening to shatter it.
A magical trap flings a character into the Far Realm until the end of that character's next turn.

entries.name: Prolonged Effects
entries: Exposure to mental stress can cause prolonged effects. Consider the following possibilities.

entries.name: Short-Term Effects
entries: The character has the {@condition Frightened|srd52}, {@condition Incapacitated|srd52}, or {@condition Stunned|srd52} condition for {@dice 1d10} minutes. This condition might be accompanied by alarming behavior or hallucinations. These effects can be suppressed with the {@spell Calm Emotions|srd52} spell or removed by the {@spell Lesser Restoration|srd52} spell.

entries.name: Long-Term Effects
entries: The character has {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on some or all ability checks for {@dice 1d10 × 10} hours, stemming from an unwillingness or inability to exert a particular set of abilities. The character might feel enervated and unable to exert much Strength, for example, or become so suspicious of others that Charisma checks are more difficult. These effects can be suppressed with the Calm Emotions spell or removed by the Lesser Restoration spell.

entries.name: Indefinite Effects
entries: An indefinite effect is a long-term effect (see above) that lasts until removed by a {@spell Greater Restoration|srd52} spell. It can be suppressed by a Calm Emotions spell.

entries.name: Poison
entries: Given their insidious and deadly nature, poisons are a favorite tool among assassins and evil creatures.
Poisons come in the following four types:

items.name: Contact
items.entry: Contact poison can be smeared on an object and remains potent until it is touched or washed off. A creature that touches contact poison with exposed skin suffers its effects.

items.name: Ingested
items.entry: A creature must swallow an entire dose of ingested poison to suffer its effects. The dose can be delivered in food or a liquid. You may decide that a partial dose has a reduced effect, such as allowing {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on the saving throw or dealing only half as much damage on a failed save.

items.name: Inhaled
items.entry: Poisonous powders and gases take effect when inhaled. Blowing the powder or releasing the gas subjects creatures in a 5-foot {@variantrule Cube [Area of Effect]|srd52|Cube} to its effect. The resulting cloud dissipates immediately afterward. Holding one's breath is ineffective against inhaled poisons, as they affect nasal membranes, tear ducts, and other parts of the body.

items.name: Injury
items.entry: Injury poison can be applied as a Bonus Action to a weapon, a piece of ammunition, or similar object. The poison remains potent until delivered through a wound or washed off. A creature that takes Piercing or Slashing damage from an object coated with the poison is exposed to its effects.

entries.name: Purchasing Poison
entries: In some settings, laws prohibit the possession and use of poison, but an illicit dealer or unscrupulous apothecary might keep a hidden stash. Characters with criminal contacts might be able to acquire poison easily. Other characters might have to make extensive inquiries and pay bribes before they acquire the poison they seek.

entries.name: Harvesting Poison
entries: A character can attempt to harvest poison from a venomous creature that is dead or has the {@condition Incapacitated|srd52} condition. The effort takes {@dice 1d6} minutes, after which the character makes a {@dc 20} Intelligence ({@skill Nature|srd52}) check using a {@item Poisoner's Kit|srd52}. On a successful check, the character harvests enough poison for a single dose, and no additional poison can be harvested from that creature. On a failed check, the character is unable to extract any poison. If the character fails the check by 5 or more, the character is subjected to the creature's poison.

entries.name: Sample Poisons
entries: Example poisons are detailed here in alphabetical order. Each poison's description includes the suggested price for a single dose of the poison, its type (contact, ingested, inhaled, or injury), and a description of the poison's debilitating effects.

entries.name: Traps
entries: Traps should be used sparingly, lest they lose their charm. A hidden pit can be a fun surprise, but too many traps in an adventure can lead players to become overly cautious, which slows down the game.

The best traps are fleeting distractions that skilled characters can overcome in a short amount of time or deadly puzzles that require quick thinking and teamwork to overcome. Traps that are undetectable and inescapable are rarely fun.

entries.name: Parts of a Trap
entries: The description of a trap includes the following parts after the trap's name:

items.name: Severity and Levels
items.entry: A trap is designated as a nuisance or as deadly for characters of certain levels. A nuisance trap is unlikely to kill or seriously harm characters of the indicated levels, whereas a deadly trap can grievously damage characters of the indicated levels.

items.name: Trigger
items.entry: Traps are often set to go off when a creature enters an area or touches an object. Examples of triggers include stepping on a pressure plate, crossing a trip wire, turning a doorknob, or using the wrong key in a lock.

items.name: Duration
items.entry: Some traps have durations expressed in rounds, minutes, or hours. Others specify that their effects last until the trap is destroyed or dispelled. If a trap's duration is instantaneous, its effect is resolved instantly.

entries: Use caution when introducing a trap to characters of a level lower than the trap's level range. A trap that is a nuisance at one level range could be deadly to characters of a lower level range.

entries.name: Example Traps
entries: Traps are presented in alphabetical order.

entries.name: Combat Encounters
entries: The following features can make a combat encounter more interesting or challenging:

items.name: Changes in Elevation
items.entry: Terrain features that provide a change of elevation (such as stacks of empty crates, ledges, and balconies) reward clever positioning and encourage characters to jump, climb, fly, or teleport.

items.name: Defensive Positions
items.entry: Enemies in hard-to-reach locations or defensive positions force characters who normally attack at range to move around.

items.name: Mixed Monster Groups
items.entry: When different types of monsters work together, they can combine their abilities—just like characters with different classes and origins. A diverse force is more powerful.

items.name: Reasons to Move
items.entry: Use features that encourage characters and their enemies to move around, such as chandeliers, kegs of gunpowder or oil, and rolling stone traps.

entries.name: Combat Encounter Difficulty
entries: Use the following guidelines to create a combat encounter of a desired level of difficulty.

entries.name: Step 1: Choose a Difficulty
entries: Three categories describe the range of encounter difficulty:

items.name: Low Difficulty
items.entry: An encounter of low difficulty is likely to have one or two scary moments for the players, but their characters should emerge victorious with no casualties. One or more of them might need to use healing resources, however. As a rough guideline, a single monster generally presents a low-difficulty challenge for a party of four characters whose level equals the monster's CR.

items.name: Moderate Difficulty
items.entry: Absent healing and other resources, an encounter of moderate difficulty could go badly for the adventurers. Weaker characters might get taken out of the fight, and there's a slim chance that one or more characters might die.

items.name: High Difficulty
items.entry: A high-difficulty encounter could be lethal for one or more characters. To survive it, the characters will need smart tactics, quick thinking, and maybe even a little luck.

entries.name: Step 2: Determine Your XP Budget
entries: Using the XP Budget per Character table, cross-reference the party's level with the desired encounter difficulty. Multiply the number in the table by the number of characters in the party to get your XP budget for the encounter.

entries.name: Step 3: Spend Your Budget
entries: Every creature has an XP value in its stat block. When you add a creature to your combat encounter, deduct its XP from your XP budget to determine how many XP you have left to spend. Spend as much of your XP budget as you can without going over. It's OK if you have a few unspent XP left over. Examples are given below:

items.name: Example 1
items.entry: A low-difficulty encounter for four level 1 characters has an XP budget of 50 × 4, for a total of 200 XP. With that, you could build any of the following encounters:

items: 2 {@creature Giant Wasp|srd52|Giant Wasps} (100 XP each), for 200 XP total
6 {@creature Twig Blight|srd52|Twig Blights} (25 XP each), for 150 XP total

items.name: Example 2
items.entry: A moderate-difficulty encounter for five level 3 characters has an XP budget of 225 × 5, for a total of 1,125 XP. With that, you could build either of these encounters:

items: 2 {@creature Nothic|srd52|Nothics} (450 XP each) and 9 {@creature Stirge|srd52|Stirges} (25 XP each), for 1,125 XP total
1 {@creature Wight|srd52} (700 XP), 1 {@creature Warhorse Skeleton|srd52} (100 XP), and 6 {@creature Skeleton|srd52|Skeletons} (50 XP each), for 1,100 XP total

items.name: Example 3
items.entry: A high-difficulty encounter for six level 15 characters has an XP budget of 7,800 × 6, for a total of 46,800 XP. With that, you could build this encounter:

items: 2 {@creature Adult Red Dragon|srd52|Adult Red Dragons} (18,000 XP each) and 2 {@creature Fire Giant|srd52|Fire Giants} (5,000 XP each), for 46,000 XP total

entries.name: Troubleshooting
entries: When creating and running combat encounters, keep the following in mind.

entries.name: Many Creatures
entries: The more creatures in an encounter, the higher the risk that a lucky streak on their part could deal more damage to the characters than you expect. If your encounter includes more than two creatures per character, include fragile creatures that can be defeated quickly. This guideline is especially important for characters of level 1 or 2.

entries.name: Adjustments
entries: A player's absence might warrant removing creatures from an encounter to keep it at the intended difficulty. Also, die rolls and other factors can result in an encounter being easier or harder than intended. You can adjust an encounter on the fly, such as by having creatures flee (making the encounter easier) or adding reinforcements (making the encounter harder).

entries.name: CR 0 Creatures
entries: Creatures that have a CR of 0, particularly ones that are worth 0 XP, should be used sparingly. If you want to include many CR 0 critters in an encounter, use swarms from the {@book Monster Manual|srd52} instead.

entries.name: Number of Stat Blocks
entries: The best combat encounters often pair one kind of creature with another, such as fire giants paired with hell hounds. Be mindful of the number of stat blocks you need to run the encounter. Referencing more than two or three stat blocks for a single encounter can be daunting, particularly if the creatures are complex.

entries.name: Powerful Creatures
entries: If your combat encounter includes a creature whose CR is higher than the party's level, be aware that such a creature might deal enough damage with a single action to take out one or more characters. For example, an {@creature Ogre|srd52} (CR 2) can kill a level 1 Wizard with a single blow.

entries.name: Unusual Features
entries: If a monster has a feature that lower-level characters can't easily overcome, consider not adding that monster to an encounter for characters whose level is lower than the monster's Challenge Rating.

data.name: Magic Items
entries: Magic items are gleaned from the hoards of felled monsters or discovered in long-lost vaults. Such items grant capabilities a character could rarely have otherwise, or they complement their owner's capabilities in wondrous ways.

entries.name: Magic Item Rules
entries: Rules for identifying, attuning to, and using magic items appear in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}". Additional rules are presented below.

entries.name: Attunement Prerequisites
entries: If a magic item has a class prerequisite, a creature must be a member of that class to attune to the item. If a creature must be a spellcaster to attune to an item, the creature qualifies if it can cast at least one spell using its traits or features, not by using a magic item or the like.

entries.name: Items Made for Specific Creatures
entries: Magic items that are meant to be worn tend to magically adjust themselves to the wearer. However, you can decide that a magic item doesn't adjust its size to fit any wearer. For example, a particular armorer might make items usable only by folk who are sized and shaped like dwarves.

entries.name: Unusual Anatomy
entries: Use your discretion to decide whether a creature can wear an item not made for its anatomy. A ring placed on a tentacle might work, but a yuan-ti with a snakelike tail instead of legs can't wear magic boots.

entries.name: Paired Items
entries: You can allow exceptions to the rule that paired items must both be worn. For example, a character with only one arm might be able to use a single {@item Gloves of Missile Snaring|srd52|Glove of Missile Snaring} so long as the matching glove is on their person.

entries.name: Magic Item Categories
entries: Every magic item belongs to a category. The Magic Item Categories table lists the nine categories and provides examples. Rules for the categories appear after the table.

entries.caption: Magic Item Categories
rows: {@item Bag of Holding|srd52}, {@item Boots of Elvenkind|srd52}

entries.name: Armor
entries: An item in the Armor category is typically a magical version of armor from "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}". Unless an armor's description notes otherwise, the armor must be worn for its magic to function.
Some suits of magic armor specify the type of armor they are, such as {@item Chain Mail|srd52} or {@item Plate Armor|srd52}. If no type is specified, choose the type or determine it randomly.

entries.name: Potions
entries: An item in the Potion category might be a magical brew that must be imbibed or an oil that must be applied to a creature or an object. A typical potion consists of 1 ounce of liquid in a vial.

entries.name: Using a Potion
entries: Potions are consumable items. Drinking a potion or administering it to another creature requires a Bonus Action. Applying an oil might take longer as specified in its description. Once used, a potion takes effect immediately, and it is used up.

entries.name: Mixing Potions
entries: A character might drink one potion while still under the effects of another or pour several potions into a single container. The strange ingredients used in creating potions can result in unpredictable interactions.

When a character mixes two potions together, roll on the Potion Miscibility table. If more than two are combined, roll again for each subsequent potion, combining the results. Unless the effects are immediately obvious, reveal them only when they become evident.

entries.caption: Potion Miscibility
rows: Both potions lose their effects, and the mixture creates a magical explosion in a 5-foot-radius {@variantrule Sphere [Area of Effect]|srd52|Sphere} centered on itself. Each creature in that area takes {@dice 4d10} Force damage.
Both potions lose their effects, and the mixture becomes an ingested poison of your choice (see "{@book Poison|srd52|10|Poison}" in "{@book Gameplay Toolbox|srd52|10}").
Both potions work, but with their numerical effects and durations halved. If a potion has no numerical effect and no duration, it instead loses its effect.
Both potions work, but the numerical effects and duration of one potion are doubled. If neither potion has anything to double in this way, they work normally.

Only one potion works, but its effects are permanent. Choose the simplest effect to make permanent or the one that seems the most fun. For example, a {@item Potion of Healing|srd52} might increase the drinker's Hit Point maximum by {@dice 2d4 + 2}, or a {@item Potion of Invisibility|srd52} might give the drinker the {@condition Invisible|srd52} condition indefinitely. At your discretion, a {@spell Dispel Magic|srd52} spell or similar magic might end this lasting effect.

entries.name: Rings
entries: For its magic to function, an item in the Ring category must be worn on a finger or a similar digit unless its description notes otherwise.

entries.name: Rods
entries: An item in the Rod category is a scepter usually made of metal, wood, or bone. A typical rod weighs 2 to 5 pounds.
Unless its description notes otherwise, a rod can be used as an {@item Arcane Focus|srd52}.

entries.name: Scrolls
entries: An item in the Scroll category is a roll of paper or parchment, sometimes attached to wooden rods and typically kept safe in a tube of ivory, jade, leather, metal, or wood. The most prevalent scroll is the {@item Spell Scroll|srd52}, a spell stored in written form.

entries.name: Using a Scroll
entries: Scrolls are consumable items. Unleashing the magic in a scroll requires the user to read the scroll. When its magic has been invoked, the scroll can't be used again. Its words fade, or it crumbles into dust.
Any creature that can understand a written language can read a scroll and attempt to activate it unless its description notes otherwise.

entries.name: Staffs
entries: Items in the Staff category vary widely in appearance: some are of nearly equal diameter throughout and smooth, others are gnarled and twisted, some are made of wood, and others are composed of polished metal or crystal. A staff weighs between 2 and 7 pounds and serves well as a walking stick or cane.
Unless its description notes otherwise, a staff can be used as a nonmagical {@item Quarterstaff|srd52} and an {@item Arcane Focus|srd52}.

entries.name: Wands
entries: An item in the Wand category is typically 12 to 15 inches long and crafted of metal, bone, or wood. It is tipped with metal, crystal, stone, or some other material.
Unless its description notes otherwise, a wand can be used as an {@item Arcane Focus|srd52}.

entries.name: Weapons
entries: A magic weapon is typically a magical version of a weapon from "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}". Some magic weapons specify the type of weapon they are in their descriptions, such as a {@item Longsword|srd52} or {@item Longbow|srd52}. If no weapon type is specified, you may choose the type or determine it randomly.

entries.name: Ammunition
entries: If a magic weapon has the {@itemProperty AF|srd52|Ammunition} property, ammunition fired from it is considered magical for the purpose of any rule that cares whether a weapon is magical or not.

entries.name: Wondrous Items
entries: Wondrous Items include wearable items such as boots, belts, capes, amulets, brooches, and circlets. Bags, carpets, figurines, horns, musical instruments, and more also fall into this category.

entries.name: Magic Item Rarity
entries: Every magic item has a rarity, which provides a rough measure of an item's power relative to other magic items. The rarities are shown in the Magic Item Rarities and Values table.
Common magic items, such as a {@item Potion of Healing|srd52}, are the most plentiful. Artifacts, such as the {@item Dragon Orb|srd52}, are priceless, unique, and difficult to acquire.

entries.name: Magic Item Values by Rarity
entries: Common magic items can often be bought in a town or city. Uncommon and Rare magic items are usually found only in cities, and rarer magic items might be sold only in wondrous locations, such as the {@book City of Brass|srd52|5|City of Brass} or {@book Sigil|srd52|5|Sigil, City of Doors}. If you allow characters to buy and sell magic items in your campaign, rarity can help you set prices for those items. Gold Piece values are provided in the Magic Item Rarities and Values table, though a seller might ask for a service rather than coin as payment.

If a magic item incorporates an item that has a purchase cost in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" (such as a weapon or a suit of armor), add that item's cost to the magic item's value. For example, {@item +1 Plate Armor|srd52|+1 Armor (Plate Armor)} has a value of 5,500 GP, which is the sum of a Rare magic item's value (4,000 GP) and the cost of {@item Plate Armor|srd52} (1,500 GP).

entries.caption: Magic Item Rarities and Values
footnotes: *Halve the value for a consumable item other than a {@item Spell Scroll|srd52}. The value of a Spell Scroll is double what it costs to scribe the scroll (as specified in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}").

entries.name: Activating a Magic Item
entries: It usually takes a {@action Magic|srd52} action to activate a magic item. The item's user might also need to do something special. The description of each item category or individual item details how an item is activated. Certain items use the following rules for their activation.

entries.name: Command Word
entries: A command word is a word or short phrase that must be spoken or signed for an item to work. Spoken command words must be audible and fail to work in areas where all sound is suppressed, as in the area of the {@spell Silence|srd52} spell.

entries.name: Consumable Items
entries: Some items are consumed—used up, in other words—when they are activated. A {@item Potion of Healing|srd52} must be swallowed, for example, while the writing vanishes from a scroll when it is read. Once used, a consumable item loses its magic.

entries.name: Spells Cast from Items
entries: Some magic items allow the user to cast a spell from the item. The spell is cast at the lowest possible spell and caster level, doesn't expend any of the user's spell slots, and requires no components unless the item's description notes otherwise. The spell uses its normal casting time, range, and duration, and the user of the item must concentrate if the spell requires {@status Concentration|srd52}. Many items, such as Potions, bypass the casting of a spell and confer the spell's effects with its usual duration. Certain items make exceptions to these rules, changing the casting time, duration, or other parts of a spell.

A magic item may require the user to use their own spellcasting ability when casting a spell from the item. If the user has more than one spellcasting ability, the user chooses which one to use with the item. If the user doesn't have a spellcasting ability, their spellcasting ability modifier is +0 for the item, and the user's Proficiency Bonus applies.

entries.name: Charges
entries: Some magic items have charges that must be expended to activate their properties. The number of charges an item has remaining is revealed when the {@spell Identify|srd52} spell is cast on it. A creature attuned to an item knows how many charges the item has and how many it regains.

entries.name: "The Next Dawn"
entries: Magic items often have charges or properties that recharge at the next dawn or some other specified time. If such an item is on a world or plane of existence where the specified event doesn't occur, the GM determines when the item recharges.

entries.name: Cursed Items
entries: A magic item's description specifies whether it bears a curse. Most methods of identifying items, including the {@spell Identify|srd52} spell, fail to reveal such a curse.
Attunement to a cursed item can't be ended voluntarily unless the curse is broken first, such as with a {@spell Remove Curse|srd52} spell.

entries.name: Magic Item Resilience
entries: A magic item is at least as durable as a nonmagical item of its kind. Most magic items, other than Potions and Scrolls, have Resistance to all damage.
An Artifact can be destroyed only in some special way. Otherwise, it is impervious to damage. Learning how to destroy an Artifact usually requires research or the completion of a quest.

entries.name: Crafting Magic Items
entries: "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" contains rules on brewing Potions of Healing and scribing Spell Scrolls. To create other magic items, follow the rules below. In these rules, "you" refers to the character crafting the magic item.

entries.name: Arcana Proficiency
entries: To craft a magic item, you and any assistants must have proficiency in the {@skill Arcana|srd52} skill.

entries.name: Tools
entries: The Magic Item Tools table lists which tool is required to make a magic item of each category. You must use the required tool to make an item and have proficiency with that tool. Any assistants must also have proficiency with it. For more {@book information on the tools|srd52|6|Tools}, see the "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}".

entries.caption: Magic Item Tools
rows: {@item Leatherworker's Tools|srd52}, {@item Smith's Tools|srd52}, or {@item Weaver's Tools|srd52} depending on the kind of armor as noted in the tools' descriptions
{@item Leatherworker's Tools|srd52}, {@item Smith's Tools|srd52}, or {@item Woodcarver's Tools|srd52} depending on the kind of weapon as noted in the tools' descriptions
{@item Tinker's Tools|srd52} or the tool required to make the nonmagical item on which the magic item is based

entries.name: Spells
entries: If a magic item allows its user to cast any spells from it, you must have all those spells prepared every day you spend crafting the item.

entries.name: Time and Cost
entries: Crafting a magic item takes an amount of time and money based on the item's rarity as shown in the Magic Item Crafting Time and Cost table.

entries.name: Work per Day
entries: For each day of crafting, you must work for 8 hours. If an item requires multiple days, those days needn't be consecutive.

entries.name: Assistants
entries: Characters can combine their efforts to shorten the crafting time. Divide the time needed to create an item by the number of characters working on it. Normally, only one other character can assist you, but the GM might allow more assistants.

entries.name: Raw Materials
entries: The cost in the table represents the raw materials needed to make a magic item. The GM determines whether appropriate raw materials are available. In a city, there is a 75 percent chance that the materials are available, and in any other settlement, that chance is 25 percent. If materials aren't available, you must wait at least 7 days before checking on the availability again.

If a magic item incorporates an item that has a purchase cost (such as a weapon or a suit of armor), you must also pay that entire cost or craft that item using the rules in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}". For example, to make {@item +1 Plate Armor|srd52|+1 Armor (Plate Armor)}, you must pay 3,500 GP or pay 2,000 GP and craft the armor.

entries.caption: Magic Item Crafting Time and Cost
footnotes: *The time and cost are halved for a consumable item other than a {@item Spell Scroll|srd52}, whose {@table Scribing Spell Scrolls; Spell Scroll Costs|srd52|crafting time and cost} are given in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}".

entries.name: Sentient Magic Items
entries: Some magic items have sentience and personality. Such an item might be possessed, haunted by the spirit of a previous owner, or self-aware thanks to the magic used to create it. A sentient item might be a cherished ally to its wielder or a continual thorn in the side.
Most sentient items are weapons, but other kinds of items can manifest sentience. Single-use items such as potions and scrolls are never sentient.

The GM controls sentient magic items and their activated properties. A bearer who maintains a good relationship with the item can access those properties. If the relationship is strained, a conflict can ensue (see "{@book Conflict|srd52|6|Conflict}" below).

entries.name: Sentient Magic Item Traits
entries: When you make a sentient magic item, you create the item's persona much as you would create an NPC, with these exceptions.

entries.name: Abilities
entries: A sentient magic item has Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma scores. Choose the item's abilities, or determine them randomly as follows: roll {@dice 4d6} for each one, dropping the lowest roll and totaling the rest.

entries.name: Alignment
entries: A sentient magic item has an alignment. Its creator or nature might suggest an alignment. Otherwise, pick an alignment or roll on the Sentient Item's Alignment table.

entries.name: Communication
entries: A sentient item communicates by sharing its emotions, broadcasting its thoughts telepathically, or speaking aloud. You can choose how it communicates or roll on the Sentient Item's Communication table.

entries.name: Senses
entries: A sentient item can perceive its surroundings out to a limited range. You can choose its senses or roll on the Sentient Item's Senses table.

entries.name: Special Purpose
entries: You can give a sentient item an objective it pursues, perhaps to the exclusion of all else. As long as the wielder's use of the item aligns with that special purpose, the item remains cooperative. Deviating from this course might cause conflict between the wielder and the item (see "{@book Conflict|srd52|6|Conflict}" below). You can pick a special purpose or roll on the Sentient Item's Special Purpose table.

entries.caption: Sentient Item's Communication
rows: The item communicates by transmitting emotion to the creature carrying or wielding it.
The item speaks one or more languages.
The item speaks one or more languages. In addition, the item can communicate telepathically with any creature that carries or wields it.

entries.caption: Sentient Item's Senses
rows: Hearing and standard vision out to 30 feet
Hearing and standard vision out to 60 feet
Hearing and standard vision out to 120 feet
Hearing and {@sense Darkvision|srd52} out to 120 feet

entries.caption: Sentient Item's Special Purpose
rows: Aligned. The item seeks to defeat or destroy those of a diametrically opposed alignment. Such an item is never Neutral.
Bane. The item seeks to thwart or destroy creatures of a particular type, such as Constructs, Fiends, or Undead.
Creator Seeker. The item seeks its creator and wants to understand why it was created.
Destiny Seeker. The item believes it and its bearer have key roles to play in future events.
Destroyer. The item craves destruction and goads its user to fight arbitrarily.
Glory Seeker. The item seeks renown as the greatest magic item in the world by winning fame or notoriety for its user.
Lore Seeker. The item craves knowledge or is determined to solve a mystery, learn a secret, or unravel a cryptic prophecy.
Protector. The item seeks to defend a particular kind of creature, such as elves or werewolves.
Soulmate Seeker. The item seeks another sentient magic item, perhaps one that is similar to itself.
Templar. The item seeks to defend the servants and interests of a particular deity.

entries.name: Conflict
entries: When the bearer of a sentient item acts in a manner opposed to the item's alignment or purpose, conflict can arise. When such a conflict occurs, the item's bearer makes a Charisma saving throw ({@dc 12} plus the item's Charisma modifier). On a failed save, the item makes one or more of the following demands:

items.name: Chase My Dreams
items.entry: The item demands that its bearer pursue the item's goals to the exclusion of all other goals.

items.name: Get Rid of It
items.entry: The item demands that its bearer dispose of anything the item finds repugnant.

items.name: It's Time for a Change
items.entry: The item demands to be given to someone else.

items.name: Keep Me Close
items.entry: The item insists on being carried or worn at all times.

entries: If its bearer refuses to comply with the item's demands, the item can do any of the following:

items: Make it impossible for its bearer to attune to it.
Suppress one or more of its activated properties.

Attempt to take control of its bearer, whereupon the bearer makes a Charisma saving throw ({@dc 12} plus the item's Charisma modifier). On a failed save, the bearer has the {@condition Charmed|srd52} condition for {@dice 1d12} hours. While Charmed in this way, the bearer must try to follow the item's commands. If the bearer takes damage, it repeats the save, ending the effect on a success. Whether or not the attempt to control its bearer succeeds, the item can't use this power again until the next dawn.

data.name: Magic Items A-Z
entries: Magic items are presented in alphabetical order.

If a magic item description capitalizes a creature's name and presents it in {@b bold} type, that's a visual cue pointing you to the creature's stat block. Unless the text states otherwise, the stat block is in "{@book Monsters|srd52|13}". How to read and use a stat block is explained in "{@book Monsters|srd52|13}".

items: {@item Amulet of Proof against Detection and Location|srd52}

entries.name: Stat Block Overview
entries: A monster has a stat block that contains the rules necessary to use it in the game. Stat blocks are divided into the following parts, which correspond with the example stat block, Vampire Familiar:

items.name: Name and General Details
items.entry: The name of the monster is followed by its size, creature type (along with any descriptive tags), and alignment.

items.name: Combat Highlights
items.entry: {@variantrule Armor Class|srd52}, {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52}, {@variantrule Speed|srd52}, and {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} are provided here.

items.name: Ability Scores
items.entry: A monster's ability scores, ability modifiers, and saving throws are listed here.

items.name: Other Details
items.entry: The monster's Senses, Languages, and CR entries appear here. Additional details appear in some monsters, such as skill proficiencies, Resistances, Immunities, and Gear. If a monster lacks those details, entries for them don't appear.

items.name: Traits
items.entry: Monster characteristics that are active at all times or during certain situations appear here.

items.name: Actions
items.entry: The monster can take the actions here in addition to those in "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}".

items.name: Bonus Actions
items.entry: This section provides a monster's Bonus Actions, if any.

items.name: Reactions and Legendary Actions
items.entry: These sections provide Reactions and Legendary Actions, if any. The example monster doesn't include these parts.

entries.name: Parts of a Stat Block
entries: The rules for a stat block are detailed in "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}" and in this section.

entries.name: Size
entries: A monster is Tiny, Small, Medium, Large, Huge, or Gargantuan. If size options are presented, you choose the creature's size from those options. See "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" for information on size.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: Each monster has a tag that identifies the type of creature it is. Certain spells, magic items, class features, and other effects in the game interact in special ways with creatures of a particular type.
The game includes the following creature types, which have no rules of their own:

items.name: {@filter Aberrations|bestiary|type=aberration}
items.entry: are utterly alien beings, such as aboleths, beholders, flumphs, and mind flayers.

items.name: {@filter Beasts|bestiary|type=beast}
items.entry: are non-Humanoid natural creatures, like horses and wolves, as well as most giant animals.

items.name: {@filter Celestials|bestiary|type=celestial}
items.entry: are magical creatures, such as angels and pegasi, with ties to the Upper Planes.

items.name: {@filter Constructs|bestiary|type=construct}
items.entry: are magically created creatures such as homunculi, modrons, and shield guardians.

items.name: {@filter Dragons|bestiary|type=dragon}
items.entry: are scaly beings of ancient origin, such as red dragons and wyverns.

items.name: {@filter Elementals|bestiary|type=elemental}
items.entry: are beings from the Elemental Planes, such as efreet and water elementals.

items.name: {@filter Fey|bestiary|type=fey}
items.entry: are creatures tied to the Feywild or the forces of nature, such as dryads, goblins, and pixies.

items.name: {@filter Fiends|bestiary|type=fiend}
items.entry: are creatures tied to terrifying Lower Planes, such as balors and hell hounds.

items.name: {@filter Giants|bestiary|type=giant}
items.entry: are towering beings with humanlike shapes, like cyclopes, fire giants, and trolls.

items.name: {@filter Humanoids|bestiary|type=humanoid}
items.entry: are people defined by their roles and professions, such as mages, pirates, and warriors. They include members of varied species.

items.name: {@filter Monstrosities|bestiary|type=monstrosity}
items.entry: are unnatural creatures with strange origins, such as mimics and owlbears.

items.name: {@filter Oozes|bestiary|type=ooze}
items.entry: are gelatinous creatures, including black puddings and blobs of annihilation.

items.name: {@filter Plants|bestiary|type=plant}
items.entry: are sentient vegetation and fungal monsters, such as myconids, shambling mounds, and treants.

items.name: {@filter Undead|bestiary|type=undead}
items.entry: are spirits and the reanimated dead, such as ghosts, vampires, and zombies.

entries.name: Descriptive Tags
entries: A monster might have one or more tags in parentheses following its type. Such tags provide additional categorization and have no rules of their own, but certain game effects might refer to them.

entries.name: Alignment
entries: The alignment specified in a monster's stat block is a default suggestion of how to roleplay the monster, inspired by its traditional role in the game or real-world folklore. Change a monster's alignment to suit your storytelling needs. The Neutral alignment, in particular, is an invitation for you to consider whether an individual leans toward one of the other alignments.
"{@book Character Creation|srd52|2}" describes the nine alignments and unaligned creatures.

entries.name: Armor Class
entries: A monster's {@variantrule Armor Class|srd52} (AC) includes its natural armor, Dexterity, gear, and other defenses. See "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" for information on Armor Class.

entries.name: Initiative
entries: The {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} entry specifies the monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} modifier followed by the monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} score in parentheses. Use the modifier when you roll to determine a monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52}. A monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} modifier is typically equal to its Dexterity modifier, but some monsters have additional modifiers, such as {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus}, applied to that number.

If you don't want to roll a monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52}, use the {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} score as the monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} in combat. Initiative is further detailed in "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}".

entries.name: Hit Points
entries: A monster's {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} are presented as a number followed by parentheses, where the monster's {@variantrule Hit Point Dice|srd52} are provided, along with any contribution from its Constitution. Either use the number for the monster's {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} or roll the die expression in parentheses to determine the monster's {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} randomly; don't use both.
A monster's size typically determines the die used to calculate its {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52}, as shown in the Hit Dice by {@variantrule Size|srd52} table.

A monster's Constitution modifier is multiplied by the number of Hit Dice it possesses, and the result is added to its {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52}. For example, if a monster has a Constitution of 12 (+1 modifier) and {@dice 2d8} Hit Dice, it has {@dice 2d8 + 2} {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} (average 11).
For more on Hit Points, see "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}".

entries.name: Speed
entries: The Speed entry specifies a monster's Speed. Some monsters have one or more of the following speeds: {@variantrule Burrow Speed|srd52|Burrow}, {@variantrule Climb Speed|srd52|Climb}, {@variantrule Fly Speed|srd52|Fly}, {@variantrule Swim Speed|srd52|Swim}. Rules for Speed and these specials speeds appear in "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}".

entries.name: Ability Scores
entries: Every monster has six ability scores along with corresponding ability score modifiers and saving throw modifiers. For more information on ability scores and saving throws, see "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}".

entries.name: Skills
entries: The Skills entry specifies a monster's skill proficiencies, if any. For example, a monster that is very perceptive and stealthy might have bonuses to Wisdom ({@skill Perception|srd52}) and Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|srd52}) checks. A skill bonus is the sum of a monster's relevant ability modifier and its {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus}. Other modifiers might apply.

entries.name: Resistances and Vulnerabilities
entries: These entries list a monster's Resistances and Vulnerabilities, if any. See "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" for more information.

entries.name: Immunities
entries: This entry lists the monster's {@variantrule Immunity|srd52|Immunities}, if any. If the monster has damage and condition Immunities, the damage types are listed before the conditions. See "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" for details.

entries.name: Gear
entries: Monsters have proficiency with their equipment. If a monster has equipment that can be given away or retrieved, the items are listed in the Gear entry. The monster's stat block might include special flourishes that happen when the monster uses an item, and the stat block might ignore the rules in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" for that item. When used by someone else, a retrievable item uses its "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" rules, ignoring any special flourishes in the stat block.
The Gear entry doesn't necessarily list all of a monster's equipment. For example, a monster that wears clothes is assumed to be dressed appropriately, and those clothes aren't in this entry.
Equipment mentioned outside the Gear entry is considered to be supernatural or highly specialized, and it is unusable when the monster is defeated.

entries.name: Ammunition and Ranged Attacks
entries: A monster that requires ammunition to make ranged attacks carries the necessary ammunition.

entries.name: Equipping a Monster with Other Items
entries: You may equip monsters with additional gear however you like, using the items in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}" for inspiration. You decide how much of a monster's equipment is recoverable after the creature is slain and whether any of that equipment is still usable.

Beware of giving a monster combat-oriented magic items, since those might alter the monster's {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52}. If you do give a monster a magic item, the monster can have {@variantrule Attunement|srd52} with magic items as noted in "{@book Equipment|srd52|6}". A monster with a class tag after its creature type is considered a member of that class for {@variantrule Attunement|srd52} purposes.

entries.name: Running a Monster
entries: To ensure a monster acts in accordance with its {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52}, follow these rules during combat:

items.name: Special Abilities
items.entry: If the monster has a special ability that deals a lot of damage but has a limited number of uses, such as a recharging breath weapon or a spell it can cast only once per day, have it use that special ability as quickly and as often as possible.

items.name: Multiattack
items.entry: If the monster has Multiattack, have it use Multiattack on any of its turns in which it's not using one of its more powerful abilities.

items.name: Bonus Actions, Reactions, Legendary Actions
items.entry: If the monster has Bonus Actions, Reactions, or Legendary Actions in its stat block, make sure it uses them as often as it can.

entries.name: Senses
entries: The Senses entry specifies a monster's {@variantrule Passive Perception|srd52} score, as well as any special senses the monster possesses. Passive Perception and special senses are described in "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}".

entries.name: Languages
entries: This entry lists languages that the monster can use to communicate. Sometimes a monster can understand a language but can't communicate with it, which is noted in its entry. "None" indicates that a creature doesn't comprehend any language.

entries.name: Telepathy
entries: Telepathy is a magical ability that allows a creature to communicate mentally with another creature within a specified range. See "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}" for more information.

entries.name: Challenge Rating
entries: Challenge Rating is defined in "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}", while guidance on using CR to plan potential combat encounters is in "{@book Gameplay Toolbox|srd52|10}".

entries.name: Experience Points
entries: The number of {@variantrule Experience Points|srd52} (XP) a monster is worth is based on its CR, as detailed in the {@variantrule Experience Points|srd52} by {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52} table. XP is awarded for defeating the monster in combat or otherwise neutralizing it.
Unless a rule says otherwise, a monster summoned by a spell or another magical ability is worth the XP noted in its stat block.

entries.name: Proficiency Bonus
entries: A monster's {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus} (PB) is determined by its CR, as shown in the {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus} by {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52} table, and is reflected in saving throws, skills, and other statistics where the monster's exceptional aptitude is a factor.

entries.name: Traits
entries: A monster's traits, if any, are features that are active at all times or in certain situations.

entries.name: Actions
entries: A monster can take the actions in this section or take one of the actions available to all creatures, as described in "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}".

entries.name: Attack Notation
entries: The entry for a monster's attack identifies whether the attack is a melee or a ranged attack and then provides the attack roll's bonus, its reach or range, and what happens on a hit. An attack is against one target unless its entry says otherwise. For details on different kinds of attacks, see "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" and "{@book Spells|srd52|7}".

entries.name: Hit
entries: Any damage dealt or other effects that occur as a result of an attack hitting a target are described after the "Hit:" notation.

entries.name: Miss
entries: If an attack has an effect that occurs on a miss, that information follows the "Miss:" notation.

entries.name: Hit or Miss
entries: If an attack has an effect that occurs regardless of whether it hits or misses its target, that information follows the "Hit or Miss:" notation.

entries.name: Saving Throw Effect Notation
entries: If an effect forces a saving throw, the effect identifies the kind of save required and then provides the save's DC, a description of which creatures make the save, and an explanation of what happens on a failed or successful save.
"Half damage only" on a successful save means the target takes half as much damage (round down) as targets that fail the save, while also ignoring all other parts of the effect.

entries.name: Damage Notation
entries: A stat block usually provides both a number and a die expression for each instance of damage. For example, an attack might deal 4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) damage on a hit. You decide whether to use the number or the die expression in parentheses; don't use both.

entries.name: Multiattack
entries: Some creatures can make more than one attack when they take the {@action Attack|srd52} action. Such creatures have the Multiattack entry in the "Actions" section of their stat block. This entry details the attacks a creature can make, as well as any additional abilities it can use, as part of the {@action Attack|srd52} action.

entries.name: Spellcasting
entries: If a monster can cast any spells, its stat block lists the spells and provides the monster's spellcasting ability, spell save DC (if any spells require a saving throw), and spell attack bonus (if any spells require an attack roll). Unless noted otherwise, a spell of level 1 or higher is always cast at its lowest possible level and can't be cast at a higher level.

A monster's spell can have special rules or restrictions. For example, a green hag can cast the {@spell Invisibility|srd52} spell, but the spell has a "self only" restriction, which means the spell affects only the hag.

entries.name: Spell Components
entries: The Spellcasting trait notes whether the monster's spellcasting ignores the need for certain spell components. If any spell components are required, describe the monster's use of Verbal, Somatic, or Material components to signal to characters that it is casting a spell. A monster that requires Material components has them.

entries.name: Casting Times of 1+ Minutes
entries: If a spell has a casting time of 1 minute or more yet is listed in a spellcasting action, the monster doesn't cast the spell in just one action unless the action's description states otherwise; the monster must take the {@action Magic|srd52} action on each of its turns and maintain {@status Concentration|srd52} to cast the spell, as described in "{@book Rules Glossary|srd52|9}".

entries.name: Bonus Action
entries: If a monster has Bonus Action options, they are listed in this section. See "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" for details on Bonus Actions.

entries.name: Reactions
entries: If the monster has Reaction options, those are listed in this section along with their triggers. See "{@book Playing the Game|srd52|1}" for details on Reactions.

entries.name: Legendary Actions
entries: If the monster has Legendary Action options, those are listed in this section. A Legendary Action is an action that a monster can take immediately after another creature's turn. Only one of these actions can be taken at a time and only after another creature's turn ends. The monster can't take a Legendary Action if it has the {@condition Incapacitated|srd52} condition or is otherwise unable to take actions.

The monster has a limited number of Legendary Action uses, and that number is specified in the stat block. The monster expends one use whenever it takes a Legendary Action, and it regains all expended uses at the start of each of its turns.

entries.name: Limited Usage
entries: Some parts of a stat block have restrictions on the number of times they can be used. Here are the most common ways that usage is limited:

items.name: X/Day
entries: This notation means the stat block part can be used a certain number of times (represented by X) and that a monster must finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} to regain expended uses. For example, a {@variantrule Reaction|srd52} that includes "1/Day" means the {@variantrule Reaction|srd52} can be taken once and that the monster must finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} to take it again.

items.name: Recharge X–Y
entries: This notation means a monster can use the stat block part once. At the start of each of the monster's turns, roll {@dice 1d6}. If the roll is within the number range given in the notation (represented by X–Y), the monster regains the use of that part, which also recharges when the monster finishes a {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52}. For example, "Recharge 5–6" in an action means a monster can take the action once. Then, at the start of each of the monster's turns, it regains the use of that action if it rolls a 5 or 6 on {@dice 1d6}.

items.name: Recharge after a Short or Long Rest
entries: This notation means the monster can use the stat block part once and must then finish a {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} to use it again.
